They are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and to rank the features they would prioritize (e.g., sound quality, ease of use, bundled accessories).. Sample: 300 participants (150 creators, 150 individual buyers) from home-studio communities and social media platforms.. Measure: 1) Average maximum price participants indicate they would pay for each product. 2) Share of participants who select 'sound quality' as the top priority. 3) Share of participants who select 'ease of use' as the top priority.. Test "Activity-specific vs sustainability differentiated proposition test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A offers a differentiated product for outdoor recreation (comfort and activity-specific features) with a price of €45. Condition B offers a differentiated product for outdoor recreation with sustainability features (eco-friendly materials, carbon-neutral production) at the same price. Both conditions include a brief description of the product and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.. Sample: 500 adult consumers aged 18-45, recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions.. Measure: WTP (maximum amount participants would pay) and purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition A than in Condition B.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition B than in Condition A.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least €10, proceed to develop the activity-specific differentiated proposition. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least €10, proceed to develop the sustainability differentiated proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), do not invest in either differentiated proposition and continue focusing on existing B2B markets.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Functional vs Status Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with boats or yachts. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) functional messaging emphasizing marine safety, durability, and protection; (B) status messaging emphasizing brand prestige, luxury, and lifestyle. After viewing the message, participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) to ensure statistical power and detect meaningful differences.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher average maximum price in the functional messaging condition compared to the status messaging condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher average maximum price in the status messaging condition compared to the functional messaging condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the functional condition exceeds the status condition by at least 1.5 points on the 1‑10 scale, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional marine safety. Test "Jotun Consumer Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two parallel paths. Participants are recruited from marine enthusiasts and homeowners/DIY users. Each path presents a different product proposition and purchase option. Path A presents Jotun’s marine and protective coatings as a premium, performance-focused product with direct-to-consumer purchase. Path B presents Jotun’s decorative and protective coatings as an affordable, high-quality finish for residential projects with retail purchase through Jotun’s Multicolor Centers. Participants are asked to indicate their willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 10% above competitor price) and to purchase. The test measures purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 marine enthusiasts and 250 homeowners/DIY users, recruited via online panels to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and willingness to pay premium (percentage above competitor price).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium in Path A (marine enthusiasts) compared to Path B (homeowners/DIY users).; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium in Path B (homeowners/DIY users) compared to Path A (marine enthusiasts).. Decision rule: If Path A’s purchase intent and willingness to pay premium are at least 15 percentage points higher than Path B’s, conclude T1 is more likely. If Path B’s purchase intent and willingness to pay premium are at least 15 percentage points higher than Path A’s, conclude T2 is more likely. If neither difference meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting marine enthusiasts and individual boat owners, leveraging Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology. The evidence shows Jotun already offers direct-to-consumer sales and has a presence in marine markets, but there is no direct evidence of consumer awareness or willingness to pay a premium. Conduct the proposed test to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Value proposition: A premium, performance-focused marine and protective coating line that demonstrates superior durability, safety, and brand reputation, sold directly to consumers at a price justified by quality.. Favoured theory: T1. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and stated willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent than Group A.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for Group A exceeds Group B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 45% vs 35%), proceed with a health-focused consumer proposition. Test "Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-45 who have purchased hearing protection in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: Lifestyle Condition (stylish, comfortable design, free at concert entry), Safety Condition (safety certification for specific high-risk activity, mandatory requirement), and Control Condition (no messaging). In each condition, participants are shown a product description of a hearing protection item (Hellberg Junior) and asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per condition), recruited from an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and hearing protection purchase history.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for the Hellberg Junior product in each condition.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle Condition will achieve a purchase intent score at least 20 points higher than Safety Condition.; T2: Safety Condition will achieve a purchase intent score at least 20 points higher than Lifestyle Condition.. Decision rule: If Lifestyle Condition’s purchase intent score is at least 20 points higher than Safety Condition’s, conclude T1 is more supported. If Safety Condition’s purchase intent score is at least 20 points higher than Lifestyle Condition’s, conclude T2 is more supported. If neither difference meets the 20‑point threshold, the evidence is insufficient to distinguish between the two theories and the recommendation will be to conduct further testing.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, emphasizing style, comfort, and free provision at entry points. This aligns with evidence that consumers are willing to change behaviour when hearing protection is provided for free and presented as a fashion item. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, emphasizing style, comfort, and free provision at entry points. This aligns with evidence that consumers are willing to change behaviour when hearing protection is provided for free and presented as a fashion item. Target customer: Consumers aged 18-45 who purchase hearing protection for leisure activities such as concerts, outdoor recreation, and everyday use.. Value proposition: A stylish, comfortable hearing protection product that meets safety standards, sold at a premium price point, with the option to purchase multiple pairs for different activities.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate purchase intent differences and refine messaging before full-scale rollout.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for hearing protection and the willingness to pay a premium for a lifestyle proposition are uncertain. Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Status" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from outdoor recreation and tech‑conscious demographics. Half see a safety‑focused message emphasizing emergency reliability and remote‑area protection; the other half see a status‑focused message emphasizing brand prestige and premium safety. Both groups are offered a simulated purchase of a consumer‑grade 406‑MHz PLB at a fixed price point.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited via outdoor recreation forums and tech‑focused online communities, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and stated primary reason for purchase (safety vs status). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Safety‑focused group will have higher purchase intent and WTP than status‑focused group.; T2: Status‑focused group will have higher purchase intent and WTP than safety‑focused group.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 10 percentage points and the status‑focused condition exceeds the safety‑focused condition by at least 5 percentage points, conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 5 points or the safety‑condition wins, conclude T1 is more likely. If both conditions are equal, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Value proposition: A premium‑priced consumer‑grade 406‑MHz satellite distress beacon that provides automatic, reliable emergency signaling, reducing response time and perceived risk during outdoor activities.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 10% or the status‑focused condition wins by at least 5 percentage points, we would shift focus to a status‑driven consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand or a large addressable market, we would reconsider the investment.; If regulatory hurdles or distribution challenges are identified, we would explore alternative routes to market.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.; 2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.; 4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform..

T1: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they view it as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and gardening, and they trust the brand for durability and reliability. Who benefits: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need a single tool for mowing, weeding, and light landscaping.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from multiple tools or manual labor to a single, easy‑to‑use machine that can handle multiple tasks, reducing time and effort.. How value is captured: Deere captures value by selling a differentiated consumer model at a premium price, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer superior performance and durability.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a single, integrated tool.; The market size for small‑scale landscaping is sufficient to justify production.; Deere can differentiate its lawn tractor from competitors through design and performance.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show higher intent to purchase a differentiated lawn tractor compared to a generic garden tool.; Sales of the differentiated model would be higher in regions with larger homeowner populations.; Competitor lawn tractors would show lower sales or lower market penetration in the same regions..

T2: Small‑farm owners will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they need a versatile tool for multiple tasks (mowing, weeding, light landscaping) and value the brand’s reputation for durability and reliability. Who benefits: Small‑farm owners and hobby farmers who require a single tool for various agricultural and garden tasks.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from multiple tools or manual labor to a single, easy‑to‑use machine that can handle multiple tasks, reducing time and effort.. How value is captured: Deere captures value by selling a differentiated consumer model at a premium price, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer superior performance and durability.. Assumptions: Small‑farm owners are willing to pay a premium for a versatile tool.; The market size for small‑farm owners is sufficient to justify production.; Deere can differentiate its lawn tractor from competitors through design and performance.. Predictions: A survey of small‑farm owners would show higher intent to purchase a differentiated lawn tractor compared to a generic garden tool.; Sales of the differentiated model would be higher in regions with larger small‑farm populations.; Competitor lawn tractors would show lower sales or lower market penetration in the same regions..

Test "Consumer vs Small-Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a consumer-focused proposition emphasizing convenience, single-tool functionality, and homeowner benefits; Group B receives a small-farm-focused proposition emphasizing versatility, multiple task capability, and small-farm owner benefits. Both groups are shown a product description of a differentiated lawn tractor (e.g., Deere 4010) and asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants: 150 homeowners (small‑scale gardens) and 150 small‑farm owners (hobby farmers). Recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target markets.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B.; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 2 points higher than Group B, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If Group B’s score is at least 2 points higher, proceed with a small‑farm focused proposition (supports T2). If the difference is less than 2 points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners with small gardens, leveraging the existing tractor engineering and brand reputation. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and refine the proposition before full-scale production. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners with small gardens, leveraging the existing tractor engineering and brand reputation. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and refine the proposition before full-scale production. Target customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need a single, convenient tool for mowing, weeding, and light landscaping.. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor that combines the durability and performance of a Deere tractor with a consumer-friendly design, offering a single, integrated solution for multiple tasks.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Small-Farm Messaging Test to validate purchase intent and refine the proposition.. Uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for a differentiated proposition is uncertain; the test will determine whether the demand is sufficient to justify investment.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the differentiated model is significantly lower than for a generic garden tool, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore alternative use cases or market segments.; If the test shows small-farm owners are more interested than homeowners, we would shift focus to a small-farm proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

T1: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a life-saving emergency device for remote environments, and they will purchase it if it is positioned as a premium safety tool for outdoor activities (e.g., hiking, camping, boating). Who benefits: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who need reliable signaling in remote areas where traditional communication fails.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers will shift from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they understand its unique capability to reach a distress call through satellite, offering peace of mind and higher perceived safety.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling premium-priced units directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online channels, leveraging its existing brand credibility for marine and military safety.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of the existence and purpose of 406 MHz PLBs.; Outdoor activities in remote areas (e.g., Alaska, Australia) are common enough to create demand.; Willingness to pay a premium for a specialized device is higher than for generic ELTs.; ACR can reach individual buyers through existing channels or new partnerships.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused marketing campaign to outdoor groups, purchase intent will exceed 10% among respondents who identify themselves as hikers, campers, or boating recreationists.; Surveyed consumers will cite 'safety in remote emergencies' as the top reason for purchasing the beacon, with willingness to pay at least $800..

T2: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a cost-effective, no‑regulation alternative to expensive ELTs and RFFI, and they will purchase it when price is the primary barrier to entry. Who benefits: Budget‑conscious outdoor enthusiasts, boat owners, and emergency‑prepared individuals who need a reliable signaling device without the cost of professional certification.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers will switch from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they perceive it as a cheaper, simpler solution that meets the same safety requirement without the regulatory and certification overhead.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling lower‑priced units through mass‑market channels, leveraging its existing manufacturing capabilities to produce a consumer‑focused version of its existing product line.. Assumptions: Price is the primary barrier to adoption for emergency signaling devices.; Consumers are aware of the existence of 406 MHz PLBs but do not view them as a premium product.; ACR can produce a consumer‑grade version of its existing product at a lower cost than its current B2B offerings.. Predictions: In a test offering a low‑priced consumer version of the beacon, purchase intent will be higher among respondents who cite budget constraints as their primary reason for not buying a beacon.; Surveyed consumers will cite 'cost' as the top reason for not purchasing a beacon, with willingness to pay at least $500..

Does not show: It does not show that consumers will purchase the device or that they will pay a premium for it; it only defines the device's purpose and intended use..

T2 supports, from acr-wiki-epirbcost (market_fact): "Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs) are a development of the ELT designed specifically for use on boats and ships, and basic models tend to be less expensive than ELTs (average cost is $800". Does not show: It does not show that consumers will purchase the device or that price is the primary barrier; it only indicates the price range of existing ELTs..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Premium vs. Cost-Concern Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 400 respondents (200 self-identified outdoor enthusiasts/hikers, 200 budget-conscious consumers). Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: (A) premium positioning emphasizing life-saving capability and remote emergency use; (B) cost‑concern positioning emphasizing lower price and no certification requirement. Both conditions present a $800 price point for a consumer‑grade 406 MHz beacon. Measure purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).. Sample: 400 respondents (200 outdoor enthusiasts, 200 budget‑conscious consumers) recruited via outdoor forums and general consumer panels.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).. Predictions: T1: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and at least 5% among budget‑conscious consumers; primary reason will be "safety in remote emergencies."; T2: In the cost‑concern condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and at least 5% among outdoor enthusiasts; primary reason will be "cost.". Decision rule: If purchase intent in the premium condition exceeds 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and 5% among budget‑conscious consumers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent in the cost‑concern condition exceeds 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and 5% among outdoor enthusiasts, consider a lower‑priced consumer version. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer sales.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Public sources from 2002 indicate the 406 MHz PLB is intended for life‑threatening remote emergencies and is regulated for public use, but they do not show consumer demand, willingness to pay, or whether ACR can reach individual buyers. Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent under premium and cost‑concern messaging before investing in a product Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Public sources from 2002 indicate the 406 MHz PLB is intended for life‑threatening remote emergencies and is regulated for public use, but they do not show consumer demand, willingness to pay, or whether ACR can reach individual buyers. Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to measure purchase intent under premium and cost‑concern messaging before investing in a product Target customer: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who need reliable signaling in remote areas where traditional communication fails.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon marketed as a premium safety tool for remote emergencies, leveraging ACR’s existing brand credibility for marine and military safety.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Messaging Test (400 respondents, two message conditions, $18,000 budget, 10 weeks) to determine whether purchase intent meets the thresholds before any product development.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and ACR’s ability to reach individual buyers remain uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the premium messaging condition achieves purchase intent above 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and 5% among budget‑conscious consumers, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.; If the cost‑concern messaging condition achieves purchase intent above 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and 5% among outdoor enthusiasts, we would consider a lower‑priced consumer version.; If neither condition meets its threshold, we would maintain the current B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because they view it as a safety necessity for outdoor activities (camping, hiking, boating) and are willing to pay a premium for peace of mind. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who face remote emergency situations and want reliable rescue communication.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from relying on traditional PLBs (registered with NOAA) to a consumer product that meets FCC approval and offers real-time rescue capability, reducing fear of being unreachable.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price (e.g., $700) through retail channels, capturing margin on a single-use device rather than recurring B2B services.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. are sufficient to generate a meaningful consumer market.; FCC approval and NOAA registration requirements do not deter consumers from purchasing a consumer product.; Marketing can effectively communicate the safety benefit to individual buyers.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade PLB to outdoor enthusiasts, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a B2B version of the same technology.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'emergency rescue' as the primary reason for purchase, not cost or compatibility with existing gear..

T2: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is a convenient, low‑cost alternative to traditional PLBs, and they purchase it as a one‑time safety device rather than as a recurring service. Who benefits: Cost‑conscious consumers who want a simple, affordable way to communicate in emergencies without ongoing subscription fees.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from the hassle of NOAA registration, FCC approval, and potential service costs to a plug‑and‑play device that works immediately, reducing perceived barrier to purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a consumer product at a lower price point (e.g., $400) through retail channels, capturing volume sales and margin on a disposable device rather than premium pricing.. Assumptions: Consumers perceive the complexity of PLB registration and FCC compliance as a significant barrier to purchase.; A one‑time purchase is acceptable for safety devices, especially when the device is marketed as a 'plug‑and‑play' solution.; Retail distribution channels can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer product at a lower price, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a premium B2B version of the same technology.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'cost' or 'easy setup' as the primary reason for purchase, not emergency rescue capability..

Test "Framing Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Framing (device marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management) or Fitness Framing (device marketed as a fitness tracking device). Both conditions present the same product description and price (proposed €199). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (1‑10 euros).. Sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced for age, gender, and BMI.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (continuous).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Health Framing condition compared to the Fitness Framing condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Fitness Framing condition compared to the Health Framing condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the Health Framing condition is at least 10 points higher than in the Fitness Framing condition (p < 0.05), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 10 points, recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the current B2B market.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Jotun Consumer Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two parallel paths. Participants are recruited from marine enthusiasts and homeowners/DIY users. Each path presents a different product proposition and purchase option. Path A presents Jotun’s marine and protective coatings as a premium, performance-focused product with direct-to-consumer purchase. Path B presents Jotun’s decorative and protective coatings as an affordable, high-quality finish for residential projects with retail purchase through Jotun’s Multicolor Centers. Participants are asked to indicate their willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 10% above competitor price) and to purchase. The test measures purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 marine enthusiasts and 250 homeowners/DIY users, recruited via online panels to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and willingness to pay premium (percentage above competitor price).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium in Path A (marine enthusiasts) compared to Path B (homeowners/DIY users).; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium in Path B (homeowners/DIY users) compared to Path A (marine enthusiasts).. Decision rule: If Path A’s purchase intent and willingness to pay premium are at least 15 percentage points higher than Path B’s, conclude T1 is more likely. If Path B’s purchase intent and willingness to pay premium are at least 15 percentage points higher than Path A’s, conclude T2 is more likely. If neither difference meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

the impedance value of a body to be measured vary according to the date, time and differences of body condition before measurement. These various are too large to use the above-described inference formula accurately and amount of body fat calculated by the formula is likely to be inaccurate.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).; 4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales..

T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, because they already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data. Who benefits: Home users who want to track weight and body composition for health improvement.. Why behaviour changes: If the device provides a clear, measurable health metric (body fat percentage), consumers will be motivated to purchase it as a tool to monitor progress and make informed health decisions.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated consumer product and potential recurring revenue from accessories or subscription services.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides measurable health data.; The device is accurate enough to be trusted by consumers for health decisions.; Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits to home users.. Predictions: In a test offering a home body-fat analyser to a target segment of health-conscious consumers, purchase intent and actual purchase rates will be higher than for a generic bathroom scale.; Consumers will report higher satisfaction with the device when it is framed as a health monitoring tool compared to a standard scale..

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a fitness tracking device, because they already use bathroom scales and seek activity-based health data. Who benefits: Fitness enthusiasts and health-conscious consumers who want to track weight loss progress and monitor activity.. Why behaviour changes: If the device provides real-time activity data and a clear weight loss metric, consumers will be motivated to purchase it as a tool to monitor fitness progress.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a fitness-focused consumer product and potential data-driven services or accessories.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a device that tracks both weight and activity.; The device is accurate enough to provide reliable fitness data.; Marketing can effectively communicate the fitness benefits to target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a home body-fat analyser marketed as a fitness tracker, purchase intent and actual purchase rates will be higher than for a health-focused framing.; Consumers will report higher satisfaction when the device is framed as a fitness tool compared to a health-focused framing..

Test "Framing Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Framing (device marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management) or Fitness Framing (device marketed as a fitness tracking device). Both conditions present the same product description and price (proposed €199). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (1‑10 euros).. Sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced for age, gender, and BMI.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (continuous).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Health Framing condition compared to the Fitness Framing condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Fitness Framing condition compared to the Health Framing condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the Health Framing condition is at least 10 points higher than in the Fitness Framing condition (p < 0.05), recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 10 points, recommend no expansion and continue focusing on the current B2B market.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (health monitoring) rather than a broad fitness-focused offering. The evidence shows that consumers already use bathroom scales and that Tanita's body-fat analyser has demonstrated accuracy, so a health-focused framing aligns with existing consumer behavior and the accuracy of the device. Test "Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-45, screened for prior purchase of hearing protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (fashion-focused) or Condition B (safety-focused). In Condition A, the product is described as a stylish, fashion-branded earplug for concerts and outdoor activities, emphasizing comfort and discreet design. In Condition B, the product is described as a safety-certified earplug for high-risk activities (construction, hunting, medical), emphasizing EN 352 certification and proven performance. Both conditions include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question and a purchase intent question.. Sample: 400 participants (200 per condition), recruited from an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and geographic location.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness-to-pay (EUR). Secondary measure: intent to purchase multiple pairs for different activities.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition B purchase intent ≤ 30%, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition A purchase intent ≤ 30%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude neither theory is supported. If both conditions meet their thresholds, conduct a secondary test to separate the two.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a fashion accessory or lifestyle item, targeting specific use cases such as concerts, outdoor recreation, and work. This approach leverages existing Hellberg brand positioning and can justify premium pricing through design and marketing. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-B) concerns wear comfort and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the impact of fashion messaging. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts that fashion-focused marketing drives purchase intent. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it is marketed as a fashion accessory or lifestyle item, because they currently view hearing protection as a medical necessity and are willing to change behaviour when it is presented as stylish and convenient.. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a fashion accessory or lifestyle item, targeting specific use cases such as concerts, outdoor recreation, and work. This approach leverages Hellberg’s existing brand positioning and can justify premium pricing through design and marketing. Target customer: Consumers aged 18–45 who purchase hearing protection for leisure activities, concerts, outdoor recreation, and work, and are willing to pay a premium for stylish, comfortable solutions.. Value proposition: A fashion‑branded, comfortable earplug that reduces stigma and increases willingness to purchase multiple pairs for different activities, while maintaining safety certification and brand trust.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test (400 participants, 4 weeks, €8,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under fashion and safety messaging conditions. Use the decision rule to determine whether to proceed to. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no source reads directly addresses consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the impact of fashion messaging. The simulated result (SYN-B) concerns wear comfort and does not address consumer. Would change if: If the Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test shows Condition A purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition B purchase intent ≤ 30%, we would conclude T1 is supported and proceed with a fashion‑focused proposition.; If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition A purchase intent ≤ 30%, we would conclude T2 is supported and reconsider a safety‑focused proposition.; If neither condition meets its threshold, we would conclude neither theory is supported and recommend further market research or a different route to market.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.; Alternatives must include no expansion, a differentiated home‑studio proposition, and a broader professional range.. T1: Home-studio creators value professional-grade audio quality and are willing to pay a premium for it, so a differentiated proposition (e.g., lower-cost, specialized features) would increase their purchases and capture margin. Who benefits: Home-studio creators who need high-quality equipment for professional work.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently use consumer gear; a differentiated product signals professionalism and performance, prompting them to upgrade from entry-level gear.. How value is captured: Neumann would sell a lower-cost, specialized line at a premium price, capturing higher margins than the current professional range.. Assumptions: Creators perceive price as a barrier to professional-grade equipment.; A differentiated product would be recognized as professional by creators.; Creators are willing to pay a premium for quality.. Predictions: Creators would show higher purchase intent or actual purchases of the differentiated line compared to the current professional range.; Sales of the differentiated line would be concentrated among creators rather than general consumers..

T2: Individual buyers purchase Neumann equipment primarily for status and brand prestige, not for functional performance, so a differentiated proposition would not significantly increase purchases; the premium professional line remains the primary driver of demand. Who benefits: Individual buyers who value brand prestige and status.. Test "Differentiated vs. Professional Line Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two parallel paths. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators (n=200) and individual buyers (n=200). Each group views a product description of a Neumann studio microphone. Path A: description of a differentiated home-studio line (lower-cost, specialized features). Path B: description of the current professional line. Participants then indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would purchase. The test measures whether creators show higher intent for the differentiated line and whether individual buyers show no change.. Sample: 200 home-studio creators and 200 individual buyers, recruited via relevant online panels.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and binary purchase intent (would purchase).. Predictions: T1: Creators will show higher purchase intent for the differentiated line than for the professional line.; T2: Individual buyers will show no change in purchase intent between the differentiated and professional lines.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the differentiated line among creators is at least 1.5 points higher than the professional line, proceed to develop a differentiated home-studio proposition. If individual buyers show no change in intent, keep the single professional range. If both groups show no change, no expansion is justified.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect the target consumer segment.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) for a differentiated consumer product versus a standard industrial earplug. 2) Primary purchase reason: open-ended rating on lifestyle enjoyment vs. compliance. 3) WTP: stated maximum price willing to pay for the differentiated product versus the standard industrial earplug.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated product when the primary reason is lifestyle enjoyment (e.g., 'enjoying outdoor activities').; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated product when the primary reason is compliance (e.g., 'meeting safety regulations').. Decision rule: If the differentiated product's purchase intent exceeds the standard industrial earplug's intent by at least 10 percentage points and the primary reason is lifestyle enjoyment, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If compliance is the primary reason, conduct a separate compliance-focused test. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, music, or leisure) that emphasizes lifestyle enjoyment and comfort. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer purchase motivations, lifestyle preferences, or compliance requirements. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, music, or leisure) that emphasizes lifestyle enjoyment and comfort. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Outdoor enthusiasts, music enthusiasts, and leisure activities participants who currently purchase hearing protection through industrial suppliers.. Value proposition: A lifestyle-oriented earplug that combines superior protection with comfortable design, positioning Hellberg as a premium brand for activities where enjoyment and safety are equally important.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 U.S. adults, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure purchase intent, primary purchase reason, and willingness to pay for a differentiated product versus a standard industrial earplug.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company claims and a single simulated result; no real consumer demand data was found. The test will determine whether consumers will adopt a lifestyle proposition and how much they are willing to pay.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the differentiated product is not significantly higher than for a standard industrial earplug, or if compliance is the primary purchase driver, the recommendation would shift toward a compliance-focused; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for lifestyle earplugs, the recommendation would be to develop a differentiated proposition without a test.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is framed as a mandatory safety requirement for a specific use case, professionals overcome the perceived discomfort and appearance concerns, leading to higher purchase intent and compliance.. Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Functional vs Status Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with boats or yachts. They view a product page for a marine protective coating and are presented with one of two messaging conditions: (A) functional messaging emphasizing marine safety, durability, and protection; (B) status messaging emphasizing brand prestige, luxury, and lifestyle. After viewing the page, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and state the primary reason for purchase (functional need, status/prestige, or other).. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in purchase intent.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary purchase reason (functional need, status/prestige, other).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and functional need as the primary reason than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and status/prestige as the primary reason than Condition A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Condition A is at least 1.5 points higher than Condition B (i.e., Condition A average >= Condition B average + 1.5), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional marine safety. If Condition B's average is at least 1.5 points higher, pursue a status/prestige proposition. If the difference is below 1.5 points, no. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential marine safety and outdoor equipment protection, leveraging Jotun’s marine technology and existing direct-to-consumer capabilities. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential marine safety and outdoor equipment protection, leveraging Jotun’s marine technology and existing direct-to-consumer capabilities. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts who need protection for boats, yachts, or recreational vehicles.. Value proposition: Premium-priced marine protective coatings sold directly through Jotun’s website, emphasizing functional safety, durability, and long-lasting protection.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (300 participants, 6 weeks, €18,000) to compare functional vs status messaging and determine whether purchase intent and primary reason align with T1.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the specific demand drivers (functional need vs status/prestige) remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for marine safety.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for status messaging significantly higher than functional messaging, the recommendation would shift toward a status/prestige proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or lower intent for functional messaging, the investment would be reconsidered or focused on a different use case.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing affordability, lightweight design, and suitability for marine recreational users. Group B sees a professional-focused message emphasizing compliance with RTCM standards, durability, and suitability for commercial marine users. Both groups are shown a product description of a 406 MHz consumer beacon priced at $50.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 marine recreational users (recruited via outdoor recreation forums) and 150 general consumers (recruited via online panels). Stratified to match age, gender, and geographic distribution.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and actual purchase intent (binary: would buy). Also collect stated willingness to pay (WTP) and perceived safety.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B, because the consumer message directly addresses the target segment's needs.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A, because the professional message emphasizes compliance and durability, which marine recreational users may perceive as more important.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than in Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5 vs Group B average >= 4), proceed to develop a consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer line. If purchase intent is equal or Group B wins, do not invest in a consumer line.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows ACR's 406 MHz PLB is regulated for general public use and meets safety standards, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the ability to reach individual buyers cheaply. The proposed test (Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test) is the next step to validate demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows ACR's 406 MHz PLB is regulated for general public use and meets safety standards, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the ability to reach individual buyers cheaply. The proposed test (Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test) is the next step to validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Marine recreational users who face unplanned emergencies at sea.. Value proposition: A lightweight, affordable 406 MHz consumer beacon that meets safety standards and is available through consumer retailers, offering reliable marine safety at a lower price point than professional marine equipment.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test (300 respondents, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer beacon.. Uncertainty: Consumer demand for a consumer-grade 406 MHz beacon is uncertain; willingness to pay is unknown, and the ability to reach individual buyers cheaply is unproven. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent in Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than in Group B, we would proceed to develop a consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or Group B wins, we would not invest in a differentiated consumer line.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Fashion vs Functional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults interested in hearing protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a fashion-focused message (e.g., stylish, trendy earplugs for lifestyle use) and a premium price; Condition B receives a functional, safety-focused message (e.g., essential protection for specific high-risk activities) and a premium price. Both conditions present the same product (a designed, safety-certified earplug). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum willingness to pay.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition), recruited from an online panel targeting adults aged 18–45 who have purchased hearing protection in the past 12 months.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will achieve higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A’s purchase intent is at least 10 points higher than Condition B’s purchase intent, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on fashion and premium pricing. If Condition B’s purchase intent is at least 10 points higher than Condition A’s purchase intent, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional safety messaging and premium pricing. If the difference is less than 10 points, do not commit to a differentiated proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

T1: Individual marine recreational users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon because they need reliable marine safety, and they can obtain it cheaply through consumer retailers, so ACR can capture value by selling a lower‑priced, consumer‑focused product line. Who benefits: Marine recreational users who face unplanned emergencies at sea.. Why behaviour changes: They already view marine safety as a necessity; a lightweight, affordable beacon that works in remote waters reduces perceived risk and makes rescue more likely, so they would purchase it.. How value is captured: ACR sells a consumer product line directly to marine recreational users at retail prices, bypassing the B2B channel and earning margin on each unit.. Assumptions: A significant proportion of marine recreational users can afford a consumer-grade beacon.; The device meets minimum safety requirements and is widely available through consumer retailers.; The device is perceived as safer and more reliable than existing alternatives.. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a consumer beacon will be lower than for professional marine equipment.; Purchase intent will be higher among users who have experienced or fear marine emergencies.; Sales will be concentrated in retail channels rather than through specialized marine suppliers..

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Consumer Group (target marine recreational users) or Professional Group (target commercial marine users). Each group sees a product description of a 406 MHz consumer-grade distress beacon, but the key difference is the framing: Consumer Group receives a message emphasizing personal safety, affordability, and ease of use for recreational users; Professional Group receives a message emphasizing professional reliability, compliance with RTCM standards, and suitability for commercial marine operations.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 marine recreational users (recruited via outdoor recreation forums and social media) and 150 commercial marine users (recruited via maritime trade associations and professional networks).. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Consumer Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Professional Group, because the message frames the product as a personal safety item for recreational users.; T2: Professional Group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Consumer Group, because the message frames the product as a professional-grade, compliance‑oriented device for commercial marine users.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent of the Consumer Group is at least 1.5 points higher than that of the Professional Group (i.e., Consumer Group average >= Professional Group average + 1.5), we conclude that T1 is more likely and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude that T2 is more likely and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show ACR's 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use and meets regulatory requirements, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, price sensitivity, or willingness to pay. A proposed test (Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test) is needed to validate whether marine recreational users would purchase a consumer-grade beacon at a lower, Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show ACR's 406 MHz PLB is intended for general public use and meets regulatory requirements, but they do not demonstrate consumer demand, price sensitivity, or willingness to pay. A proposed test (Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test) is needed to validate whether marine recreational users would purchase a consumer-grade beacon at a lower, Target customer: Marine recreational users who face unplanned emergencies at sea.. Value proposition: A lightweight, affordable 406 MHz distress beacon that meets safety standards and is available through consumer retailers, offering reliable marine safety for recreational users.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test (300 respondents, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer-grade beacon.. Uncertainty: Consumer demand, price sensitivity, and willingness to pay for a consumer-grade beacon are uncertain. The test will resolve whether marine recreational users would adopt a lower-priced, consumer-focused product.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent and willingness to pay for a consumer beacon are significantly lower than for professional marine equipment, we would reconsider expansion and explore alternative routes to market.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand or a large market for marine recreational safety devices, we would reconsider investing in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, not just speculate.; Consider existing consumer reach of Jotun’s coatings; if none, assess feasibility of entering that market.; Alternatives include expanding into consumer markets, targeting a different customer group, or maintaining current B2B focus.. T1: Individual boat owners and marine enthusiasts will adopt Jotun’s marine and protective coatings if they perceive them as high‑performance, durable, and trusted by professionals, because they value safety and longevity for their vessels. Who benefits: Jotun gains premium pricing and repeat purchases from individual buyers who need reliable protection for their boats.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently rely on generic or cheaper alternatives; a differentiated proposition that emphasizes marine‑grade quality and professional endorsement will shift their purchase from generic to brand‑specific products.. How value is captured: Jotun can charge higher prices for its branded coatings and capture value through direct‑to‑consumer sales and repeat purchases of specialized marine products.. Assumptions: Individual boat owners are willing to pay a premium for proven marine performance.; Jotun’s reputation in professional marine markets transfers to consumer perception.; The market size for individual boat owners is sufficient to justify investment.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated marine‑focused product at a premium price, at least 30% of surveyed individual boat owners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales conversion rate will be higher than for a generic marine product of similar price point..

T2: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts will adopt Jotun’s decorative coatings if they perceive them as stylish, easy to apply, and affordable compared to competitors, because they seek aesthetic improvement for their homes. Who benefits: Jotun gains consumer sales and brand awareness in the residential market, potentially opening new revenue streams beyond marine.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently choose decorative paints based on price and availability; a differentiated proposition that highlights design options, ease of use, and competitive pricing will shift their preference from generic to brand‑specific. How value is captured: Jotun can expand its consumer presence through direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships, and potentially licensing its decorative brand to other retailers.. Assumptions: Residential buyers are willing to pay a premium for aesthetic appeal and ease of application.; Jotun’s decorative capabilities can be effectively marketed to DIY consumers.; The residential market size is large enough to justify investment.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated decorative product at a price comparable to competitors, at least 25% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales conversion rate will be higher than for a generic decorative product of similar price point..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Marine vs Decorative" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a marine‑focused product description or a decorative‑focused product description, followed by a purchase intent question.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self‑identified individual boat owners and 250 self‑identified homeowners, recruited via panel to match age, gender, and geographic distribution.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this product?” and willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of marine‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the decorative‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).; T2: At least 25% of decorative‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the marine‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).. Decision rule: If the marine‑exposed group’s purchase intent rate exceeds the decorative‑exposed group’s rate by at least 5 percentage points and its WTP is at least €50 higher, proceed with a marine‑focused consumer proposition. If the opposite holds, proceed with a decorative‑focused proposition. events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

Who benefits: Surveyors and marine recreational users in high-risk areas who face life-threatening emergencies at sea.. Why behaviour changes: A personal emergency beacon directly reduces perceived risk and provides immediate rescue capability, creating a tangible safety benefit that drives purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price to individual buyers through retail channels, capturing value from the higher margin of direct consumer sales.. Assumptions: Life-saving success rates for PLBs in the United States are known and communicated to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a price premium for a personal emergency beacon.; ACR can reach individual buyers through retail or online channels.. Why behaviour changes: The purchase is driven by the desire to demonstrate safety, preparedness, and ownership of a high-end, premium safety device, rather than purely functional necessity.. Test "Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-55, balanced for gender and geographic region. Participants view a product description of a hearing protection earplug and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10). The product description is presented in two versions: Version A is marketed as a fashion accessory with stylish design and lifestyle appeal; Version B is marketed as a safety-critical product for high‑risk activities with certification and proven performance. Participants are randomly assigned to see either Version A or Version B before being asked about purchase intent.. Sample: 400 participants (200 per version) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each version.. Predictions: T1: Version A will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than Version B.; T2: Version B will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than Version A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Version A is at least 1.5 points higher than Version B (i.e., average A ≥ 5.5 and average B ≤ 4.0), conclude that fashion‑branded messaging drives higher purchase intent and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude that safety‑positioned messaging drives higher purchase intent and recommend a safety‑focused proposition. If the difference is not statistically significant, indicate uncertainty and suggest further testing.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Sample: 200 home-studio creators (self-identified) recruited via audio forums and social media, balanced for experience level (beginner vs. advanced).. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Health Monitoring vs Fitness Tracking" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) Health Monitoring Scale - marketed as a device that provides measurable, actionable body-fat insights for health tracking; (2) Fitness Tracking Scale - marketed as a device that offers real-time activity and weight loss progress tracking. Participants are randomly assigned to view one concept and then indicate their willingness to purchase at a premium price (e.g., 20% above standard scale price).. Sample: 300 adult respondents recruited from health-conscious and fitness-focused segments, balanced across gender and age to ensure representation.. Measure: Purchase intent measured as the percentage of respondents who indicate they would purchase the presented concept at the premium price.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the Health Monitoring Scale compared to the Fitness Tracking Scale.; T2: Higher purchase intent for the Fitness Tracking Scale compared to the Health Monitoring Scale.. Decision rule: If the Health Monitoring Scale achieves purchase intent above 30% and the Fitness Tracking Scale achieves purchase intent below 20%, conclude T1 is more supported. If the Fitness Tracking Scale achieves purchase intent above 30% and the Health Monitoring Scale achieves purchase intent below 20%, conclude T2 is more supported. If neither threshold is met, the evidence is inconclusive and further testing is recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, emphasizing measurable body-fat insights and actionable health recommendations. This aligns with the existing home scale ownership in Japan and the company’s professional market success, and it addresses a clear consumer need for health tracking. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, emphasizing measurable body-fat insights and actionable health recommendations. This aligns with the existing home scale ownership in Japan and the company’s professional market success, and it addresses a clear consumer need for health tracking. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers who want to monitor weight and body composition at home.. Value proposition: A premium‑priced home body-fat scale that provides clear, quantifiable body-fat data and suggests specific health actions, enabling consumers to track progress and make informed decisions.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (300 respondents, 6 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent for the Health Monitoring concept versus the Fitness Tracking concept.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a health‑monitoring focused scale and the competitive response from existing consumer scales remain uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% for the Health Monitoring concept, indicating weak consumer demand, the recommendation would shift toward a fitness‑tracking focused proposition or no expansion.; If the test shows purchase intent above 30% for the Fitness Tracking concept, indicating strong consumer demand, the recommendation would shift toward a fitness‑tracking focused proposition.; If new evidence from 1993 shows a large, untapped consumer market for body-fat scales, the recommendation could change to target a broader segment.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
