Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect the target consumer segment.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) for a differentiated consumer product versus a standard industrial earplug. 2) Primary purchase reason: open-ended rating on lifestyle enjoyment vs. compliance. 3) WTP: stated maximum price willing to pay for the differentiated product versus the standard industrial earplug.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated product when the primary reason is lifestyle enjoyment (e.g., 'enjoying outdoor activities').; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the differentiated product when the primary reason is compliance (e.g., 'meeting safety regulations').. Decision rule: If the differentiated product's purchase intent exceeds the standard industrial earplug's intent by at least 10 percentage points and the primary reason is lifestyle enjoyment, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If compliance is the primary reason, conduct a separate compliance-focused test. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, music, or sports) that emphasizes lifestyle enjoyment and comfort. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Use the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test to validate demand before committing to full development. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Differentiated vs Certified Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a lifestyle positioning message (stylish, comfortable, fashion accessory) and a free entry-point provision message; Condition B receives a safety-requirement positioning message (high-risk activity, mandatory certification) and a free entry-point provision message. Both conditions include a purchase intent question and a willingness-to-pay question.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18-45 recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions to ensure random assignment.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness-to-pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 20% and Condition B purchase intent < 20%, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 20% and Condition A purchase intent < 20%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude neither theory is supported. If both conditions meet their thresholds, conduct a secondary test to separate the two mechanisms.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed differentiated vs certified messaging test (Condition A vs Condition B) to empirically compare consumer response to lifestyle vs safety positioning. If Condition A meets the 20% purchase-intent threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; if Condition B meets the threshold, reconsider the safety-requirement approach. If neither meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B/ear Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Marine vs Decorative" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a marine‑focused product description or a decorative‑focused product description, followed by a purchase intent question.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self‑identified individual boat owners and 250 self‑identified homeowners, recruited via panel to match age, gender, and geographic distribution.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this product?” and willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of marine‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the decorative‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).; T2: At least 25% of decorative‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the marine‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).. Decision rule: If the marine‑exposed group’s purchase intent rate exceeds the decorative‑exposed group’s rate by at least 5 percentage points and its WTP is at least €50 higher, proceed with a marine‑focused consumer proposition. If the opposite holds, proceed with a decorative‑focused proposition. If both groups’ intent rates are equal and neither meets the 5‑point difference, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Differentiated vs. Compliant Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-55, balanced across gender and geographic regions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) style-focused, comfortable earplug marketed as a lifestyle accessory for concerts and outdoor activities; (2) compliant earplug marketed as a safety requirement for construction and hunting; (3) neutral control earplug with no messaging. All conditions present the same product description and price ($45). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per condition) to ensure statistical power and detect a 10% difference in purchase intent.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (EUR) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Style-focused condition will achieve the highest average purchase intent score (>=7.5) and willingness to pay compared to the neutral control.; T2: Compliant condition will achieve the highest average purchase intent score (>=7.5) and willingness to pay compared to the neutral control.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the style-focused condition is >=7.5 and significantly higher than the neutral control, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent score for the compliant condition is >=7.5 and significantly higher than the neutral control, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the evidence is insufficient to distinguish between the theories.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade satellite distress beacon if they experience a direct life-saving incident or are aware of rescue success rates, because the perceived risk of drowning or being unreachable motivates them to purchase the technology. Who benefits: Surveyors and marine recreational users in high-risk areas who face life-threatening emergencies at sea.. Why behaviour changes: A personal emergency beacon directly reduces perceived risk and provides immediate rescue capability, creating a tangible safety benefit that drives purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price to individual buyers through retail channels, capturing value from the higher margin of direct consumer sales.. Assumptions: Life-saving success rates for PLBs in the United States are known and communicated to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a price premium for a personal emergency beacon.; ACR can reach individual buyers through retail or online channels.. Predictions: In a survey of marine recreational users, at least 30% will report having experienced a life-threatening emergency at sea, and 15% will indicate they would purchase a personal emergency beacon if priced at $300-$500.; Willingness to pay for a consumer-grade beacon will be positively correlated with stated risk perception (e.g., likelihood of drowning)..

T2: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade satellite distress beacon if they perceive it as a status symbol or a status differentiator, because they seek to signal safety, preparedness, and ownership of a premium safety device. Who benefits: Affluent marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and early adopters who value brand prestige and social signaling.. Why behaviour changes: The purchase is driven by the desire to demonstrate safety, preparedness, and ownership of a high-end, premium safety device, rather than purely functional necessity.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price through specialty retailers or online channels, capturing value from higher margin direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning.. Predictions: In a survey of marine recreational users, at least 20% will report that they would purchase a personal emergency beacon primarily for status reasons, and 15% will indicate they would pay a price premium of $500 or more.; Purchase intent for a consumer-grade beacon will be positively correlated with stated importance of status signaling and brand prestige..

Test "Creators' Willingness-to-Pay Survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators and individual content creators. They view product mockups of Neumann studio microphones and audio interfaces, each with a different price point (e.g., €500, €1,000, €1,500). They are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and to rank the features they would prioritize (e.g., sound quality, ease of use, bundled accessories).. Sample: 300 participants (150 creators, 150 individual buyers) from home-studio communities and social media platforms.. Measure: 1) Average maximum price participants indicate they would pay for each product. 2) Share of participants who select 'sound quality' as the top priority. 3) Share of participants who select 'ease of use' as the top priority.. Predictions: T1: Creators will indicate higher maximum prices for Neumann products than for competitors, and 'sound quality' will be the top priority for a majority of participants.; T2: Creators will indicate higher maximum prices for Neumann products than for competitors, and 'ease of use' will be the top priority for a majority of participants.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price for Neumann products is at least €1,200 and 'sound quality' is the top priority for at least 60% of participants, proceed to develop a differentiated home-studio proposition. If the average maximum price is below €1,200 or 'ease of use' is the top priority for at least 60% of participants, keep the single professional range for all customers.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt hearing protection if it is positioned as a fashion accessory or comfort item, because they associate earplugs with aesthetics and comfort rather than protection. Who benefits: Consumers seeking style and comfort in hearing protection; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand differentiation.. Why behaviour changes: When earplugs are presented as fashion items or comfort devices, consumers are more willing to try them, especially if they perceive them as less obtrusive and more acceptable.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering stylish designs, comfort features, and premium pricing, and by selling directly to consumers or through fashion retailers.. Predictions: In a test offering stylish, comfortable earplugs at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for standard protection.; Consumers will report higher willingness to wear earplugs when presented as fashion accessories compared to when they are described as purely protective devices..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection if it is provided at no cost or with low cost, because they perceive it as a necessary safety measure and are willing to try it without financial barrier. Who benefits: Consumers who would otherwise avoid hearing protection due to cost; Hellberg Safety gains volume sales and brand awareness through free distribution.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is offered at no cost, consumers are more likely to try it because they view it as a safety requirement rather than a purchase decision.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by leveraging existing B2B distribution channels to offer free or low-cost products to consumers, and by building brand awareness through widespread exposure.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to purchase hearing protection at a low cost or for free.; Free distribution reduces the perceived risk of trying a new product.; Hellberg can scale free distribution without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering free or low-cost hearing protection, purchase rates will be higher than when the same product is sold at a premium price.; Consumers will report higher willingness to wear hearing protection when it is provided at no cost compared to when it is sold at a higher price..

Test "Fashion vs. Free Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a stylish/comfort-focused description of earplugs (Fashion group) or a free/no-cost description (Free group). Participants are recruited from a panel matching demographic characteristics of the target consumer segment (e.g., adults aged 18-45 interested in outdoor activities). Each participant sees one description and is asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).. Sample: 300 participants (150 per group) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and willingness to pay (WTP) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Fashion group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Free group.; T2: Free group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Fashion group.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the Fashion group is at least 1.5 points higher than the Free group (i.e., >= 5.5 out of 7), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is not statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes stylish design and comfort, targeting outdoor recreation and leisure activities. Use existing B2B distribution channels to reach individual buyers and explore direct-to-consumer sales through fashion retailers. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes stylish design and comfort, targeting outdoor recreation and leisure activities. Use existing B2B distribution channels to reach individual buyers and explore direct-to-consumer sales through fashion retailers. Target customer: Adults aged 18-45 interested in outdoor activities (hiking, cycling, concerts, school/activity) who value both protection and aesthetics.. Value proposition: Hellberg offers comfortable, stylish hearing protection that provides peace of mind without compromising style, allowing consumers to feel confident and connected while protecting their hearing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Fashion vs. Free Test (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under different exposure conditions.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no source read directly addresses consumer willingness to pay for stylish or comfortable earplugs, nor does it confirm that fashion and comfort drive purchase decisions.. Would change if: If the Fashion vs. Free Test shows a difference of at least 1.5 points in purchase intent in favor of the stylish/comfort description, we would shift toward a fashion-focused proposition.; If additional evidence shows strong consumer demand for low-cost or free hearing protection, we would reconsider a low-cost distribution strategy.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Activity-specific vs sustainability differentiated proposition test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A offers a differentiated product for outdoor recreation (comfort and activity-specific features) with a price of €45. Condition B offers a differentiated product for outdoor recreation with sustainability features (eco-friendly materials, carbon-neutral production) at the same price. Both conditions include a brief description of the product and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.. Sample: 500 adult consumers aged 18-45, recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions.. Measure: WTP (maximum amount participants would pay) and purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition A than in Condition B.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent in Condition B than in Condition A.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least €10, proceed to develop the activity-specific differentiated proposition. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least €10, proceed to develop the sustainability differentiated proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), do not invest in either differentiated proposition and continue focusing on existing B2B markets.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence does not show consumer demand for comfort or activity-specific features; the existing B2B market is well served. Conduct the proposed test to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence does not show consumer demand for comfort or activity-specific features; the existing B2B market is well served. Conduct the proposed test to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Target customer: Consumers seeking comfortable, activity-specific hearing protection for outdoor recreation, school, or hobby activities.. Value proposition: A differentiated product that combines comfort and safety tailored to specific use cases, offering peace of mind and premium pricing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 12‑week, €20,000 online survey test comparing activity‑specific comfort and sustainability differentiated propositions.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for comfort and activity‑specific features is unknown; sustainability demand is also uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows Condition A (activity‑specific comfort) achieving a statistically significant €10 premium over Condition B (sustainability), we would proceed to develop the activity‑specific proposition.; If Condition B shows a statistically significant €10 premium over Condition A, we would proceed to develop the sustainability proposition.; If neither condition reaches the €10 threshold, we would maintain the B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, construction, medical).; 2) Expand the existing hearing-protection line into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., standard earplugs for general use).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B hearing and face protection markets.; 4) Change route to market or customer group (e.g., sell directly to consumers online, partner with retailers, target a new demographic).; 5) Redesign existing products for a new use case (e.g., add comfort features for extended wear)..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it is marketed as a fashion accessory or lifestyle item, because they currently view hearing protection as a medical necessity and are willing to change behaviour when it is presented as stylish and convenient. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfortable, discreet protection for activities like concerts, outdoor recreation, and work; Hellberg Safety benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: Fashion and lifestyle framing reduce the perceived stigma of wearing earplugs and increase willingness to purchase multiple pairs for different activities.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge higher prices for stylish designs, sell through fashion retailers, and build a lifestyle brand that differentiates it from industrial protection.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view hearing protection as a medical necessity rather than a fashion item.; Fashion marketing can effectively shift consumer perception of earplugs.; Hellberg has the design and marketing capacity to create a differentiated consumer line.. Predictions: In a test offering a stylish, fashion-branded earplug at a premium price, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard industrial earplug.; Consumers will report higher willingness to purchase multiple pairs for different activities when the product is marketed as a lifestyle accessory..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it is positioned as a functional, safety-critical product for specific high-risk activities (e.g., construction, hunting, medical), because they already purchase hearing protection for those environments and trust the certification. Who benefits: Professional users and safety-conscious consumers who need reliable protection for work or high-risk hobbies; Hellberg Safety benefits by leveraging existing safety certification and selling to B2B channels.. Why behaviour changes: Safety certification and proven performance reduce perceived risk and increase willingness to purchase when the product is marketed as essential for a specific use case.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell through safety distributors, offer certification-compliant products, and charge premium prices justified by safety standards.. Assumptions: Consumers already purchase hearing protection for specific high-risk activities.; Safety certification is a trusted signal for these consumers.; Hellberg can reach safety distributors and professional users.. Predictions: In a test offering a safety-certified earplug marketed for construction or hunting, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard industrial earplug.; Consumers will be more willing to purchase multiple pairs for different high-risk activities when the product is positioned as safety-critical..

Test "Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-55, balanced for gender and geographic region. Participants view a product description of a hearing protection earplug and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10). The product description is presented in two versions: Version A is marketed as a fashion accessory with stylish design and lifestyle appeal; Version B is marketed as a safety-critical product for high‑risk activities with certification and proven performance. Participants are randomly assigned to see either Version A or Version B before being asked about purchase intent.. Sample: 400 participants (200 per version) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each version.. Predictions: T1: Version A will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than Version B.; T2: Version B will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than Version A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Version A is at least 1.5 points higher than Version B (i.e., average A ≥ 5.5 and average B ≤ 4.0), conclude that fashion‑branded messaging drives higher purchase intent and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude that safety‑positioned messaging drives higher purchase intent and recommend a safety‑focused proposition. If the difference is not statistically significant, indicate uncertainty and suggest further testing.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a fashion accessory and lifestyle item, targeting consumers who currently view earplugs as a medical necessity. This approach leverages existing Hellberg brand and design capabilities to capture premium pricing and build brand loyalty. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-B) concerns wear comfort and does not address consumer willingness to purchase a differentiated fashion-branded product. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a fashion accessory and lifestyle item, targeting consumers who currently view earplugs as a medical necessity. This approach leverages Hellberg’s existing brand and design capabilities to capture premium pricing and build brand loyalty. Target customer: Consumers aged 18‑55 who purchase hearing protection for activities such as concerts, outdoor recreation, and work, and who are willing to change behaviour when presented with stylish, convenient options.. Value proposition: A fashion‑branded hearing protection line that combines comfort, discretion, and style, offering multiple pairs for different activities and enabling premium pricing through fashion retailers.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test (400 participants, 12‑week timeline, €20,000 budget) to measure purchase intent differences between fashion‑branded and safety‑positioned messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for differentiated hearing protection and the actual willingness to pay for a fashion‑branded product are unknown. The test will resolve whether fashion messaging drives higher purchase intent than safety‑m. Would change if: If the test shows a difference of ≥ 1.5 points in favour of safety‑positioned messaging, the recommendation would shift to a safety‑focused proposition.; If the test shows no statistically significant difference, further market research would be needed to assess consumer demand for a differentiated fashion proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.

A body fat measuring apparatus for measuring body fat in a patient's body comprises apparatus for simultaneously measuring an impedance between the patient's feet, and for measuring the patient's height and the patient's weight

the impedance value of a body to be measured vary according to the date, time and differences of body condition before measurement. These various are too large to use the above-described inference formula accurately and amount of body fat calculated by the formula is likely to be inaccurate.
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.

This method is safe, noninvasive, provides rapid measurements, requires little operator skill and subject cooperation, and is portable. Further validation of this method is recommended in subjects with abnormal body composition.
The Tanita TBF-310 foot-to-foot BIA body composition analyser with the manufacturer's prediction equations is not recommended for application to individual children who are overweight and obese

Constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.; Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).; 4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales..

T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool that provides measurable, actionable insights about body fat distribution, because they seek to track progress and make informed health decisions. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who want to monitor weight and body composition at home.. Why behaviour changes: If the scale shows clear, quantifiable body-fat data and suggests specific actions (e.g., reduce fat, increase muscle), consumers will be motivated to use it regularly.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated consumer product and potential recurring revenue from accessories or subscription services for health analytics.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides measurable health insights.; Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits of body-fat measurement.; The device is accurate enough to provide reliable data for health decision-making.. Predictions: A survey of target consumers will show higher intent to purchase a home body-fat scale if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool compared to a generic scale.; Sales of a differentiated consumer product will be higher in regions where health awareness is high.; Customers will report regular use of the scale for health tracking..

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it is marketed as a fitness tracking device that provides real-time feedback on activity and weight loss progress, because they seek to monitor daily habits and achieve measurable results. Who benefits: Fitness enthusiasts and weight‑loss focused consumers who want to track progress and stay motivated.. Why behaviour changes: If the scale offers continuous data on weight and activity, consumers will be motivated to use it daily to adjust their routine and stay on track.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value through a subscription model for fitness analytics, premium pricing for a connected device, and potential partnerships with fitness apps.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a device that provides real‑time activity and weight data.; The device can be integrated with existing fitness platforms or apps.; The accuracy of activity tracking is sufficient to influence consumer behavior.. Predictions: A test group will show higher adoption rates for a fitness‑tracking focused home scale compared to a health‑monitoring focused scale.; Customers will report daily use of the scale to monitor activity and weight changes.; Sales will be higher in regions with a strong fitness culture..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Health Monitoring vs Fitness Tracking" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) Health Monitoring Scale - marketed as a body-fat tracking device providing measurable insights (e.g., fat percentage, fat distribution). (2) Fitness Tracking Scale - marketed as a real-time activity and weight loss tracking device.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18-55, recruited from a panel in Japan and the United States, balanced for gender and BMI to reflect target markets.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the Health Monitoring Scale compared to the Fitness Tracking Scale.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the Fitness Tracking Scale compared to the Health Monitoring Scale.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the Health Monitoring Scale exceeds the average purchase intent for the Fitness Tracking Scale by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on health monitoring. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conduct a follow-up test to explore the fitness tracking concept.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, providing measurable body-fat insights. This aligns with existing consumer scale adoption in Japan and the company’s medical evidence base. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the stand-on body-fat analyser as a health monitoring tool, providing measurable body-fat insights. This aligns with existing consumer scale adoption in Japan and the company’s medical evidence base. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers aged 18‑55 who seek to monitor weight and body composition at home.. Value proposition: A premium‑priced home scale that delivers clear, actionable body-fat data, enabling informed health decisions and tracking progress.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 adults, 6 weeks, €15,000) to compare health‑monitoring and fitness‑tracking concepts. Use the 1.5‑point decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a health‑monitoring focused product.. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for health‑monitoring insights. If the difference in purchase intent is less than 1.5 points, the fitness‑tracking concept may be explored.. Would change if: If the test shows the fitness‑tracking concept achieving a 1.5‑point advantage over health‑monitoring, the recommendation would shift to a fitness‑tracking focused consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for real‑time activity and weight data, the recommendation would be revised to prioritize a fitness‑tracking focused product.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Neumann should create a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers beyond its existing professional studio range, or keep a single professional range for all customers, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.; Alternatives must include no expansion, a differentiated home‑studio proposition, and a broader professional range.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑studio proposition (e.g., lower‑cost, specialized features) for individual creators.; 2) Keep a single professional range for all customers (no differentiation).; 3) No expansion: continue current product mix without new propositions.; 4) Expand into adjacent segments (e.g., gaming, mobile audio) while retaining the professional line.; 5) Partner with or sell through existing consumer channels (e.g., Amazon, online retailers) to reach individual buyers..

T1: Home-studio creators value professional-grade audio quality and are willing to pay a premium for it, so a differentiated proposition (e.g., lower-cost, specialized features) would increase their purchases and capture margin. Who benefits: Home-studio creators who need high-quality equipment for professional work.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently use consumer gear; a differentiated product signals professionalism and performance, prompting them to upgrade from entry-level gear.. How value is captured: Neumann would sell a lower-cost, specialized line at a premium price, capturing higher margins than the current professional range.. Assumptions: Creators perceive price as a barrier to professional-grade equipment.; A differentiated product would be recognized as professional by creators.; Creators are willing to pay a premium for quality.. Predictions: Creators would show higher purchase intent or actual purchases of the differentiated line compared to the current professional range.; Sales of the differentiated line would be concentrated among creators rather than general consumers..

T2: Individual buyers purchase Neumann equipment primarily for status and brand prestige, not for functional performance, so a differentiated proposition would not significantly increase purchases; the premium professional line remains the primary driver of demand. Who benefits: Individual buyers who value brand prestige and status.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers already associate Neumann with professional quality; a differentiated line would not change their purchase decision because the brand signal remains the primary motivator.. How value is captured: Neumann would maintain its premium pricing and brand positioning, capturing value through high-margin professional sales rather than volume from individual buyers.. Assumptions: Brand prestige is the primary purchase driver for individual buyers.; A differentiated line would not increase purchase frequency or volume among individual buyers.; The premium professional line remains the primary revenue source.. Predictions: Individual buyers would not show increased purchase intent or actual purchases of a differentiated line.; Sales of the differentiated line would be concentrated among professional users rather than individual creators..

If the average purchase intent for specialized messaging is at least 1.5 points higher than for stylish messaging (p < 0.05), conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Purchase Intent Survey by Use Case" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Monitoring (positioned as a weight management tool) or Fitness Tracking (positioned as a fitness companion). Both conditions present a home body-fat analyser with a price point and a purchase intent question (1‑10 scale).. Sample: 500 adults aged 18‑95 in the United States, recruited via an online panel, stratified by gender and income to ensure representation.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent in the Health Monitoring condition compared to the Fitness Tracking condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent in the Fitness Tracking condition compared to the Health Monitoring condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the Health Monitoring condition is at least 5 points higher than in the Fitness Tracking condition (i.e., Health Monitoring ≥ Fitness Tracking + 5 points), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for weight management. If the difference is less than 5 points, the test is inconclusive and further market research is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

If the test shows a meaningful premium over fitness-focused messaging, proceed with a consumer product; otherwise, reconsider the expansion strategy. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. T1: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a life-saving emergency device for remote environments, and they will purchase it if it is positioned as a premium safety tool for outdoor activities (e.g., hiking, camping, boating). Who benefits: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who need reliable signaling in remote areas where traditional communication fails.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers will shift from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they understand its unique capability to reach a distress call through satellite, offering peace of mind and higher perceived safety.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling premium-priced units directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online channels, leveraging its existing brand credibility for marine and military safety.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of the existence and purpose of 406 MHz PLBs.; Outdoor activities in remote areas (e.g., Alaska, Australia) are common enough to create demand.; Willingness to pay a premium for a specialized device is higher than for generic ELTs.; ACR can reach individual buyers through existing channels or new partnerships.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused marketing campaign to outdoor groups, purchase intent will exceed 10% among respondents who identify themselves as hikers, campers, or boating recreationists.; Surveyed consumers will cite 'safety in remote emergencies' as the top reason for purchasing the beacon, with willingness to pay at least $800..

T2: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a cost-effective, no‑regulation alternative to expensive ELTs and RFFI, and they will purchase it when price is the primary barrier to entry. Why behaviour changes: Buyers will switch from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they perceive it as a cheaper, simpler solution that meets the same safety requirement without the regulatory and certification overhead.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling lower‑priced units through mass‑market channels, leveraging its existing manufacturing capabilities to produce a consumer‑focused version of its existing product line.. Assumptions: Price is the primary barrier to adoption for emergency signaling devices.; Consumers are aware of the existence of 406 MHz PLBs but do not view them as a premium product.; ACR can produce a consumer‑grade version of its existing product at a lower cost than its current B2B offerings.. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions of the same 406 MHz beacon: (A) premium positioning emphasizing life-saving capability in remote emergencies and high safety value; (B) cost‑focused positioning emphasizing lower price, no‑regulation alternative to ELTs and RFFI. After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 from outdoor recreation groups (hikers, campers, boating) and 150 from marine recreational users. Recruit via outdoor recreation forums and marine recreation associations.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay. Secondary measure: primary reason for not buying (safety vs. cost).. Predictions: T1: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among outdoor recreation respondents, and the top reason will be 'safety in remote emergencies'.; T2: In the cost‑focused condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among marine recreational respondents, and the top reason will be 'cost'.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in the premium condition exceeds 10% among outdoor recreation respondents and the top reason is 'safety in remote emergencies', proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent in the cost‑focused condition exceeds 10% among marine recreational respondents and the top reason is 'cost', develop a lower‑priced consumer version. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer market.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Differentiated vs Generic Earplug Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., outdoor recreation earplug with EN 352 certification and comfort features) or a generic earplug. They are then asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale), willingness to pay (EUR), and likelihood to purchase multiple pairs for different activities.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–45, recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in gender, age, and geographic location.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score for the differentiated product. Secondary measures: willingness to pay (EUR) and likelihood to purchase multiple pairs.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the differentiated product compared to the generic earplug.; T2: No significant difference in purchase intent between the differentiated and generic products; willingness to pay is higher for the differentiated product.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the differentiated product is at least 10 points higher than for the generic product (i.e., differentiated intent ≥ 7.5), proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, conduct further testing to refine the product.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it is marketed as a medical-grade tool for professional use, because clinics and health clubs already use Tanita equipment and trust the brand, creating a perceived credibility that transfers to home users. Why behaviour changes: Clinics and health clubs already purchase and rely on Tanita scales for clinical accuracy, so a consumer version would be seen as a compatible, trusted extension of that equipment, reducing perceived risk and increasing willingness to adopt. Test "Fashion vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults interested in hearing protection. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for a hearing protection earplug: (A) Fashion/Comfort description emphasizing style, comfort, and aesthetic appeal; (B) Compliance description emphasizing safety standards, legal requirement, and suitability for specific activities (e.g., construction, outdoor recreation). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the Fashion/Comfort condition compared to the Compliance condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the Compliance condition compared to the Fashion/Comfort condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the Fashion/Comfort condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the Compliance condition, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent for the Compliance condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the Fashion/Comfort condition, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is within 1.5 points or both conditions show similar intent, the evidence is inconclusive and further testing is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious consumers (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (health monitoring) or Condition B (fitness tracking). In Condition A, the product description emphasizes health benefits and weight management. In Condition B, the product description emphasizes fitness tracking and real-time activity data. Both conditions include a brief description of the device's technical capability and price point. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the primary reason for purchase.. Sample: 300 health-conscious consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and income levels.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase reason (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and purchase intent will be driven by health monitoring messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and purchase intent will be driven by fitness tracking messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score in Condition A is at least 5 points higher than in Condition B (i.e., Condition A ≥ Condition B + 5), we conclude that the health monitoring message (T1) is more effective. If the difference is less than 5 points, we conclude that the fitness tracking message (T2) is more effective. If the difference is not statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude that neither message is significantly more effective than the other.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

Sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a broad consumer base.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and WTP (dollar amount). Secondary measure: primary purchase reason (comfort, sustainability, other).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the activity-specific comfort description than for the sustainability description.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the sustainability description than for the activity-specific comfort description.. T1: Consumers will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they treat lawn and garden tasks as a consumer chore, and Deere can capture value by selling a branded, differentiated unit at a premium through independent dealers, leveraging its engineering reputation to command higher prices. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small gardeners benefit from a dedicated tool for their chores; Deere benefits from premium pricing and brand extension into consumer markets.. Why behaviour changes: Growing household garden size and interest in DIY in the 1960s create demand for a dedicated lawn tractor; consumers shift from generic tools to branded, differentiated products for convenience and status.. How value is captured: Deere sells a consumer-focused tractor through dealers at higher prices than its generic tractors, and can extend its brand into new markets, potentially increasing total revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded, differentiated lawn tractor.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and sell a new consumer product.; Deere's engineering reputation allows it to command premium prices.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated consumer lawn tractor to a subset of homeowners will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than a generic tractor.; Sales of the differentiated unit will generate higher average revenue than sales of a generic unit sold through the same dealers..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Status vs. Utility" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A (status-oriented) and Group B (utility-oriented). Each group sees a product description of a differentiated consumer lawn tractor (e.g., a branded, feature-rich unit) and is asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The test also includes a control group receiving a generic tractor description.. Sample: 300 participants, 100 per group, recruited from a panel of homeowners and small gardeners in the United States. Recruitment is limited to those who have owned a lawn tractor or plan to purchase one within the next 12 months.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for the differentiated unit.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group B, indicating that status-driven demand drives purchase.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group A, indicating that status-driven demand drives purchase.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 7.5 and Group B’s average ≤ 2.5), conclude that status-driven demand (T2) is the dominant driver. If the difference is less than 5 points, conclude that utility-driven demand (T1) is the dominant driver. If both groups’ average scores are within 5 points of each other, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping or homeowner tasks) using the existing tractor platform. Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Status" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from outdoor recreation and tech‑conscious demographics. Half see a safety‑focused message emphasizing emergency reliability and remote‑area protection; the other half see a status‑focused message emphasizing brand prestige and premium safety. Both groups are offered a simulated purchase of a consumer‑grade 406‑MHz PLB at a fixed price point.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited via outdoor recreation forums and tech‑focused online communities, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and stated primary reason for purchase (safety vs status). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Safety‑focused group will have higher purchase intent and WTP than status‑focused group.; T2: Status‑focused group will have higher purchase intent and WTP than safety‑focused group.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 10 percentage points and the status‑focused condition exceeds the safety‑focused condition by at least 5 percentage points, conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 5 points or the safety‑condition wins, conclude T1 is more likely. If both conditions are equal, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting marine recreational users and outdoor enthusiasts, emphasizing safety and emergency reliability. Use the proposed Consumer Messaging Test to validate demand before full product development. License the 406 MHz technology to third-party manufacturers if consumer demand is low, to capture value through royalties rather than direct sales. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Target customer: Marine recreational users and outdoor enthusiasts who need reliable emergency signaling in remote areas.. Value proposition: A premium-priced consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon that provides a clear, reliable emergency signal, reducing response time and perceived risk during outdoor activities.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Messaging Test (300 participants, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for safety versus status messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the willingness to pay a premium for a safety device are uncertain. The test will resolve whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 10% or the status message wins by at least 5 percentage points, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore licensing.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a premium safety device, we would shift focus to a differentiated consumer product line.. Test "Differentiated vs Functional Consumer Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase offer.. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via social media and music forums, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 2) Willingness to pay (WTP) for each attribute (comfort, style, performance). 3) Preferred product category (lifestyle vs functional).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for lifestyle attributes (comfort, style) than for functional attributes.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for functional attributes (performance, reliability) than for lifestyle attributes.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for lifestyle attributes exceeds the average WTP for functional attributes by at least 10% (e.g., lifestyle WTP ≥ functional WTP + 10%), conclude T1 is supported. If functional WTP exceeds lifestyle WTP by at least 10%, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is <5%, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Safety vs Trust Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Safety Condition (safety-focused messaging emphasizing marine hazards and protective coatings as a medical necessity) or Trust Condition (trust-focused messaging emphasizing brand reputation, quality, and existing consumer distribution). Both conditions present the same product (Jotun marine and protective coating) at a fixed price point.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the marine and protective coating. Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and repeat purchase intent (binary: would repurchase).. Predictions: T1: Safety Condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Trust Condition.; T2: Trust Condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Safety Condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in the Safety Condition is at least 10% higher than in the Trust Condition, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP in the Trust Condition is at least 10% higher than in the Safety Condition, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10% points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
Of the "10" series John Deere tractors introduced in 1960, the 4010 was by far the most popular, with more than 58,000 units sold from 1960 to 1963.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.; Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.. Both groups see the same price point and a. Sample: 300 homeowners aged 25-55 with small gardens, recruited via an online panel. Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: self-reported importance of status vs. utility.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A.. Who benefits: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and individuals in remote areas who need reliable emergency communication.. Why behaviour changes: The Federal Register rule (2002) and NOAA guidelines make compliance mandatory, creating a regulatory barrier that only a certified device can clear, prompting consumers to choose a trusted brand over generic alternatives.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium-priced, certified product through retail channels, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and the FCC waiver that allowed type certification for consumer use.. T2: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it offers convenience and real-time tracking, enabling them to stay connected with loved ones and receive rescue notifications, and they are willing to pay for the added safety and peace of mind. Who benefits: Travelers, outdoor workers, and families in remote areas who need continuous communication and rescue awareness.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of GPS and satellite communication makes real-time tracking desirable; consumers seek devices that provide continuous location updates and rescue notifications, creating a demand for a beacon that goes beyond a one-time emergency.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by positioning the beacon as a smart safety device with tracking and rescue capabilities, selling it through consumer electronics retailers and offering subscription services for real-time updates.. Assumptions: Consumers value continuous location tracking and rescue notifications over a single emergency signal.; The price premium for tracking features is acceptable for safety-conscious buyers.; ACR can integrate tracking software and data services into the product.. Predictions: In a test offering a tracked 406 MHz beacon at a price comparable to a standard PLB, purchase intent among outdoor workers will be at least 20% higher than for a non-tracked generic beacon.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary purchase drivers..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Emergency vs Tracking Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing life-saving emergency capability (NOAA certification, RTCM compliance, suitable for remote or life-threatening situations). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes continuous tracking and real-time rescue notifications (GPS, location updates, rescue alerts). Both groups see a price point 20% above a generic PLB (e.g., €150). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state the primary purchase driver.. Sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced across gender and age to reflect marine recreational and outdoor user demographics. Recruitment targets individuals who have used a personal locator beacon or are interested in emergency safety gear.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase driver (open-ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (price sensitivity).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, and the majority of Group A buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary drivers.; T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Group A, and the majority of Group B buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary drivers.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than Group B, adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition (emergency capability). If Group B purchase intent ≥ 20% points higher than Group A, adopt T2‑driven consumer proposition (tracking/continuous). If the difference is ≤ 10% points, no expansion is recommended. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs. Small-Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 homeowners with small gardens and 200 small-farm owners. Randomly assign participants to one of two message groups: Homeowner group receives a chore-focused proposition (e.g., 'Easily maintain your small garden with a Deere lawn tractor—save time and effort!'); Small-farm group receives a farming-focused proposition (e.g., 'Increase efficiency and reduce labor costs with a Deere small-farm lawn tractor'). Both groups view a product description of the same intended consumer model (e.g., a 1962-style Deere lawn tractor). Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑10 scale.. Sample: 400 respondents (200 homeowners, 200 small-farm owners) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑10 scale.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP than small-farm owners, indicating demand for a chore-focused proposition.; T2: Small-farm owners will show higher purchase intent and WTP than homeowners, indicating demand for a farming-focused proposition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent of the Homeowner group is at least 10 points higher than that of the Small-farm group, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent of the Small-farm group is at least 10 points higher than that of the Homeowner group, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners with small gardens, leveraging the existing tractor engineering and independent dealer network. The evidence shows a 76% rise in lawn and garden equipment sales and the 4010's popularity, but it does not confirm homeowner demand for a chore-focused proposition. A targeted test is needed to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home-Studio Creators" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators and individual audio enthusiasts. They view product descriptions of Neumann studio microphones and studio monitors, and are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay for each product. The survey also includes a brief demographic question to ensure participants are individual buyers.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 home-studio creators (self-identified) and 150 individual audio enthusiasts. Recruitment via social media groups, forums, and professional audio communities.. Measure: Maximum price willingness to pay (WTP) for each product, and a binary question: "Would you purchase this product if it were priced at your WTP?". Predictions: T1: Home-studio creators will show higher WTP for Neumann products than individual buyers, and the difference will be statistically significant.; T2: Individual buyers will show higher WTP for Neumann products than home-studio creators, and the difference will be statistically significant.. Decision rule: If the average WTP of home-studio creators for Neumann products is at least 20% higher than that of individual buyers, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP of individual buyers for Neumann products is at least 20% higher than that of home-studio creators, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, neither theory is strongly supported; if the difference is greater than 20 percentage points, conclude the opposite theory is supported. If the average WTP of both groups is similar (difference < 10 percentage points), neither theory is strongly supported and further testing is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Differentiated vs. Compliant Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-55, balanced across gender and geographic regions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) style-focused, comfortable earplug marketed as a lifestyle accessory for concerts and outdoor activities; (2) compliant earplug marketed as a safety requirement for construction and hunting; (3) neutral control earplug with no messaging. All conditions present the same product description and price ($45). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per condition) to ensure statistical power and detect a 10% difference in purchase intent.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (EUR) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Style-focused condition will achieve the highest average purchase intent score (>=7.5) and willingness to pay compared to the neutral control.; T2: Compliant condition will achieve the highest average purchase intent score (>=7.5) and willingness to pay compared to the neutral control.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the style-focused condition is >=7.5 and significantly higher than the neutral control, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent score for the compliant condition is >=7.5 and significantly higher than the neutral control, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the evidence is insufficient to distinguish between the theories.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Fashion vs. Free Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a stylish/comfort-focused description of earplugs (Fashion group) or a free/no-cost description (Free group). Participants are recruited from a panel matching demographic characteristics of the target consumer segment (e.g., adults aged 18-45 interested in outdoor activities). Each participant sees one description and is asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).. Sample: 300 participants (150 per group) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and willingness to pay (WTP) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Fashion group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Free group.; T2: Free group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Fashion group.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the Fashion group is at least 1.5 points higher than the Free group (i.e., >= 5.5 out of 7), conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is not statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes stylish design and comfort, targeting outdoor recreation and leisure activities. Use existing B2B distribution channels to reach individual buyers and explore direct-to-consumer sales through fashion retailers. Conduct a small-scale test (e.g., Fashion vs. Free Test) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes stylish design and comfort, targeting outdoor recreation and leisure activities. Use existing B2B distribution channels to reach individual buyers and explore direct-to-consumer sales through fashion retailers. Conduct a small-scale test (e.g., Fashion vs. Free Test) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Adults aged 18-45 interested in outdoor activities (hiking, cycling, concerts, school activities) who value aesthetics and comfort in hearing protection.. Value proposition: Hellberg offers stylish, comfortable earplugs that combine protection with fashion appeal, providing peace of mind and a premium experience for consumers who seek both safety and style.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Fashion vs. Free Test (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the Fashion group shows a ≥1.5-point higher average intent, proceed to develop a stylish/comfort-focused product line;. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no source directly measures consumer willingness to pay for stylish or comfortable earplugs. The test will resolve whether fashion and comfort drive purchase decisions.. Would change if: If the Fashion vs. Free Test shows no significant difference in purchase intent (difference <1.5 points), indicating T2 is supported, we would reconsider a low-cost/free distribution strategy and explore alternative value propositions.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Homeowner Preference Test: Single vs Multiple Tools" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated lawn tractor positioned as a single, integrated tool for small-scale landscaping. Group B sees the same description but positioned as a tool that reduces the number of tools needed to purchase and maintain. Both groups view a generic garden tool. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and whether they would purchase the product.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness. Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and binary purchase decision (yes/no). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium over a generic tool.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group B, because homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group A, because homeowners seek a single, integrated tool that reduces the number of tools they need to purchase and maintain.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5 and Group B’s average ≤ 1.5), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent scores between Group A and Group B is at least 1.5 points (e.g., Group A average ≥ 5.5 and Group B average ≤ 4.0), conclude the differentiated proposition aligns with the respective theory and justify investment. Test "Consumer Messaging Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious consumers (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (health monitoring) or Condition B (fitness tracking). In Condition A, the product description emphasizes health benefits and weight management. In Condition B, the product description emphasizes fitness tracking and real-time activity data. Both conditions include a brief description of the device's technical capability and price point. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the primary reason for purchase.. Sample: 300 health-conscious consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and income levels.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase reason (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and purchase intent will be driven by health monitoring messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and purchase intent will be driven by fitness tracking messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score in Condition A is at least 5 points higher than in Condition B (i.e., Condition A ≥ Condition B + 5), we conclude that the health monitoring message (T1) is more effective. If the difference is not statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude that neither message is significantly more effective than the other.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.
