Test "Creators' Willingness-to-Pay Survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators and individual content creators. They view product mockups of Neumann studio microphones and headphones, and are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay for each product, and to rank importance of features such as professional-grade sound, ease of use, and integrated features.. Sample: 300 participants (150 creators, 150 individual buyers) from home-studio and content creation communities, recruited via social media and audio forums.. Measure: Average maximum price willingness to pay (EUR) for each product, and average importance ratings for each feature.. Predictions: T1: Creators will show higher average maximum price willingness to pay for Neumann products than for competitor products, and will rank professional-grade sound as the most important feature.; T2: Creators will show higher average maximum price willingness to pay for Neumann products that emphasize ease of use and integrated features than for competitor products, and will rank ease of use as the most important feature.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price willingness to pay for Neumann products is at least 20% higher than the average maximum price for competitor products (e.g., 30% higher), and the importance of professional-grade sound is rated as the top feature by at least 60% of creators, proceed to develop a differentiated home-studio proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or ease of use is rated as the top feature by at least 60% of creators, keep the single professional range.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition that emphasizes professional-grade sound, reliability, and premium pricing, targeting committed creators who value performance. Use the proposed survey test to validate willingness to pay and feature importance before committing to product development. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Value proposition: A premium, professional-grade Neumann product that delivers superior sound and reliability, justified by the brand's reputation and the creators' need for high-quality output.. Test "Fashion vs. Free Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a fashion/comfort-focused earplug description or a free/no-cost offer for the same product.. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Test "Safety vs Trust Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Both conditions present the same product (Jotun marine and protective coating) at a fixed price point.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the marine and protective coating. Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and repeat purchase intent (binary: would repurchase).. Predictions: T1: Safety Condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Trust Condition.; T2: Trust Condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than Safety Condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in the Safety Condition is at least 10% higher than in the Trust Condition, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP in the Trust Condition is at least 10% higher than in the Safety Condition, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10% points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Functional vs Status Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with boats or yachts. They view a product page for a marine protective coating and are presented with one of two messaging conditions: (A) functional messaging emphasizing marine safety, durability, and protection; (B) status messaging emphasizing brand prestige, luxury, and lifestyle. After viewing the page, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and state the primary reason for purchase (functional need, status/prestige, or other).. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in purchase intent.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary purchase reason (functional need, status/prestige, other).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and functional need as the primary reason than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and status/prestige as the primary reason than Condition A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Condition A is at least 1.5 points higher than Condition B (i.e., Condition A average >= Condition B average + 1.5), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional marine safety. If Condition B's average is at least 1.5 points higher, pursue a status/prestige proposition. If the difference is below 1.5 points, no. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for residential marine safety and outdoor equipment protection, leveraging Jotun’s marine technology and existing direct-to-consumer capabilities. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and messaging before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts who need protection for boats, yachts, or recreational vehicles in residential marine environments.. Value proposition: Premium-priced marine protective coatings sold directly through Jotun’s website, emphasizing functional durability, safety, and long‑term protection, supported by Jotun’s brand reputation and existing distribution network.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and actual purchase intent remain uncertain; the test will resolve this. Additionally, price sensitivity and competitive positioning are unknown.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for status messaging significantly higher than functional messaging, the recommendation would shift toward a status‑focused proposition.; If the test difference is below 1.5 points, the investment would be reconsidered or the pilot would be expanded with additional messaging variations.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by pricing differentiated products at a premium, selling through specialized channels (outdoor retailers, online), and leveraging its brand reputation for safety and comfort.. Test "Differentiated Consumer Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 adults (18+), 250 parents of children under 12. Recruit via panel to match demographics.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this product for a specific use case?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP: "How much would you pay for this product?" (open-ended). 3) Messaging preference: "Which positioning resonates most?" (EN 352 safety vs. fashion accessory).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for a product positioned as EN 352-compliant hearing protection for outdoor recreation.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for a product positioned as a fashion accessory (e.g., colorful design, shareable) for children and outdoor enthusiasts.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the EN 352 positioning is at least 15 percentage points higher than for the fashion accessory positioning, proceed with a differentiated safety-focused proposition. If the difference is <5 points, consider a differentiated proposition but validate further. If neither positioning achieves the 15-point threshold, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Homeowner Preference Test: Single vs Multiple Tools" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated lawn tractor positioned as a single, integrated tool for small-scale landscaping. Group B sees the same description but positioned as a tool that reduces the number of tools needed to purchase and maintain. Both groups view a generic garden tool. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and whether they would purchase the product.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness. Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and binary purchase decision (yes/no). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium over a generic tool.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group B, because homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group A, because homeowners seek a single, integrated tool that reduces the number of tools they need to purchase and maintain.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5 and Group B’s average ≤ 1.5), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging John Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959, lawn and garden equipment sales rose 76% in 1960‑39, and the 4010 model was the most popular in the 10‑series. These points support the idea that homeowners will adopt a single, integrated tool for small tasks. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address homeowner preferences for a differentiated lawn tractor. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging John Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959, lawn and garden equipment sales rose 76% in 1960‑39, and the 4010 model was the most popular in the 10‑series. These points support the idea that homeowners will adopt a single, integrated tool for small tasks. Target customer: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need a single tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor that combines the durability and performance of a tractor with a user‑friendly design, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Homeowner Preference Test (300 homeowners, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent and conversion rates for a differentiated lawn tractor versus a generic garden tool.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay a premium and the size of the small‑scale landscaping market are uncertain. The test will clarify whether homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution.. Would change if: If the test shows a purchase intent difference of ≤ 1.5 points between the two groups, indicating no significant preference, the investment would be reconsidered.; If new evidence shows strong demand for a single, integrated tool among homeowners who already own multiple garden tools, T2 would become more likely.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product if it is marketed as a lifestyle accessory that combines comfort, style, and situational awareness, because they currently view hearing protection as a medical necessity and are willing to change behaviour when provided free at entry points. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfortable, stylish protection for activities like concerts, outdoor recreation, and work; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is presented as a fashion item and comfort item, consumers overcome the perceived discomfort and appearance concerns, leading to higher purchase intent and repeat use.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium price for a differentiated product and capture value through brand extension, direct-to-consumer sales, and repeat purchases of multiple styles.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is required by law or workplace policy, consumers comply to avoid penalties and ensure safety, leading to higher purchase and compliance rates.. How value is captured: Hellberg can secure contracts with safety managers, offer compliance-certified products, and capture value through recurring B2B sales and certifications.. Assumptions: Regulatory requirements for hearing protection exist and are enforced in target markets.; Workers and employers are willing to pay a premium for compliant products.; Hellberg can obtain the necessary certifications and market the product as compliant.. Test "Safety vs Protection Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Sample: Proposed sample: 500 participants (250 per condition) from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection.. Test "Consumer vs Small‑Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A (homeowners) receives a message emphasizing a single, convenient tool for small‑scale landscaping and gardening, while Group B (small‑farm owners) receives a message emphasizing a versatile tool for multiple tasks. Both groups view the same lawn tractor model (e.g., 4010) and are asked about purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑10).. Sample: 500 participants: 250 homeowners and 250 small‑farm owners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for the differentiated lawn tractor.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B.; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 2 points higher than Group B, we conclude that homeowners are the primary target and support T1. If Group B's score is at least 2 points higher, we conclude small‑farm owners are the primary target and support T2. If the difference is less than 2 points, we conclude neither theory is supported and recommend further market research.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs Small-Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a consumer-focused proposition emphasizing convenience, single-tool functionality, and homeowner benefits; Group B receives a small-farm-focused proposition emphasizing versatility, multiple task capability, and small-farm owner benefits. Both groups are shown a product description of a differentiated lawn tractor (e.g., Deere 4010) and asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants: 150 homeowners (small‑scale gardens) and 150 small‑farm owners (hobby farmers). Recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target markets.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B.; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 2 points higher than Group B, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If Group B’s score is at least 2 points higher, proceed with a small‑farm focused proposition (supports T2). If the difference is less than 2 points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Who benefits: Consumers seeking protection at events; Hellberg gains sales through distribution partners.. Why behaviour changes: Free access removes perceived cost barrier and reduces appearance concerns, making protection acceptable even without personal financial investment.. How value is captured: Hellberg captures value by selling through partners at event locations, earning a margin on each unit sold.. Assumptions: Free provision at events is feasible for Hellberg's current distribution model.; Partners will promote Hellberg's products at events.; Consumers are willing to purchase when the product is offered free.. Predictions: In a test where hearing protection is provided free at events, purchase rates will be higher than when sold at a price.; Surveyed consumers will report higher intent to purchase when the product is offered free..

T2: Consumers purchase hearing protection when it is marketed as a lifestyle accessory or fashion item, leading to multiple purchases for different activities. Who benefits: Fashion-conscious consumers and lifestyle brands; Hellberg gains brand equity and multiple sales channels.. Why behaviour changes: When protection is framed as stylish or suitable for various activities, consumers view it as a personal accessory rather than a utilitarian item, increasing purchase frequency.. How value is captured: Hellberg can sell multiple units through different channels (online, retail, event partners) and capture premium pricing based on design and brand perception.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with fashion and lifestyle.; Hellberg can design and market products that appeal to fashion-conscious buyers.; Retail and online channels can be leveraged to reach these consumers.. Predictions: In a test where hearing protection is marketed as a fashion accessory, purchase rates will be higher than when marketed as a functional product.; Consumers will report higher intent to purchase when the product is framed as stylish..

Test "Free vs Fashion Framing Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two versions of a hearing protection product description: (1) free at events with emphasis on protection and standard compliance; (2) fashion accessory with emphasis on style and multiple activity suitability. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18-45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to reflect Europe.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay for each framing.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay when protection is framed as free at events.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay when protection is framed as a fashion accessory.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the free framing version exceeds the fashion framing version by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed with a differentiated free-at-events proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition; consider a. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated free-at-events proposition for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation or concerts) rather than a broad fashion marketing campaign. T1 kept: The simulated result shows that a styled protector increases wear frequency, which supports the idea that appearance matters for consumer adoption. New claim: Consumers purchase hearing protection when it is marketed as a stylish, fashion accessory that can be worn across multiple activities, leading to multiple purchases.. Evidence: SYN-C.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated free-at-events proposition for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation or concerts) rather than a broad fashion marketing campaign. Target customer: Consumers attending events where hearing protection is needed (concerts, outdoor activities, construction sites) and who currently lack a convenient, affordable option.. Value proposition: Provide a comfortable, stylish hearing protection solution that is free at events, removing the cost barrier and appearance concern, leading to higher adoption and repeat purchases.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Free vs Fashion Framing Test (500 adults, 6 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and willingness to pay under free and fashion framing. Use the 1.5-point difference rule to decide whether to proceed with a free-at-ev. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether free provision drives actual purchases, and whether consumers will pay a premium for a differentiated product. Market demand for a specific use case is also uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows the free framing version does not outperform the fashion framing version by at least 1.5 points, or if purchase intent is low even when free, we would reconsider the investment.; If new evidence shows that price sensitivity is a dominant factor, we would explore a lower-priced proposition or a different route to market.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by leveraging existing B2B distribution channels to offer free or low-cost products to consumers, and by building brand awareness through widespread exposure.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to purchase hearing protection at a low cost or for free.; Free distribution reduces the perceived risk of trying a new product.; Hellberg can scale free distribution without compromising margins.. Test "Homeowner Preference Test: Single vs Multiple Tools" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated lawn tractor offering a single, integrated tool for small-scale landscaping. Group B sees the same description but emphasizes multiple tools and the ability to purchase separate attachments. Both groups are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state their primary reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness. Participants must have a small garden (e.g., up to 1,000 square feet) and be interested in gardening or landscaping.. Measure: Primary measure is the average purchase intent score for Group A (differentiated single-tool proposition) versus Group B (multiple-tool proposition). Secondary measure is the proportion of respondents who cite convenience/single-tool preference as their reason for choosing the product.. Why behaviour changes: When consumers view hearing protection as a necessary item for a particular activity (e.g., hunting, shooting, construction), they are motivated to purchase it to meet safety standards and avoid legal or health consequences.. How value is captured: Hellberg can position products as activity-specific safety gear and sell through industry-focused channels (e.g., outdoor retailers, safety suppliers) that serve the target demographic.. Assumptions: There is a measurable demand for hearing protection in specific high-risk activities.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for products that meet activity-specific safety standards.; Safety regulations or industry standards drive purchase decisions for these activities.. Test "Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two groups: Lifestyle Group (n=200) and Safety Group (n=200). Each group views a product description of the same hearing protection item (e.g., a lifestyle-branded earplug for outdoor activities). Lifestyle Group sees a description emphasizing style, activity alignment, and comfort. Safety Group sees a description emphasizing EN 352 certification, activity-specific protection, and compliance with safety standards. Both groups are asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 400 adult consumers aged 18–45, recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in gender, age, and geographic location.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle Group will have a purchase intent score at least 15 points higher than Safety Group, and willingness to pay will be at least 10% higher for the lifestyle-branded version.; T2: Safety Group will have a purchase intent score at least 15 points higher than Lifestyle Group, and willingness to pay will be at least 10% higher for the safety-branded version.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between Lifestyle and Safety Groups is at least 15 points and the difference in willingness to pay is at least 10%, we conclude that the respective theory is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points in either intent or willingness to pay, we conclude neither theory is supported. If both groups show similar intent and willingness to pay, we conclude no significant difference.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs B2B PLB Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Participants view a product page for a Jotun marine coating (identical product description and price). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Safety-focused (emphasizing marine safety and protective coatings) or Protection-focused (emphasizing protection from marine elements and chemical damage). After viewing the page, participants indicate purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The test is run in two rounds with a 12-week interval to capture any repeat purchase behavior.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) recruited from an online panel targeting homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts in Scandinavia and the UK.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Safety-focused condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Protection-focused condition.; T2: Protection-focused condition will generate higher purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Safety-focused condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the Safety-focused condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the Protection-focused condition, conclude T1 is more likely. If the average purchase intent score for the Protection-focused condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the Safety-focused condition, conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is recommended.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it provides a clear, actionable health message and is marketed as a personal wellness tool, because health awareness in the 1990s makes them willing to invest in devices that measure body fat for weight management. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking to manage weight and improve health.. Why behaviour changes: Increased media coverage of health risks (heart disease, diabetes) and the availability of portable devices make consumers view body fat as a measurable health metric, prompting purchase for personal use.. How value is captured: Tanita would capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated consumer product and potential recurring revenue from accessories or subscription services for health tracking.. Assumptions: Consumers in 1993 are motivated by health concerns and are willing to pay for devices that provide measurable outcomes.; Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits of body fat measurement to home users.; The technology can be adapted to a consumer-friendly form factor without compromising accuracy.. Predictions: A survey of target consumers would show at least 30% indicating intent to purchase a home body-fat scale for weight management.; Sales of a consumer version would exceed 5,000 units within the first year in a key market (e.g., Japan or the US)..

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it is marketed as a medical-grade tool for professional use, because clinics and health clubs already use Tanita equipment and trust the brand, creating a perceived credibility that transfers to home users. Who benefits: Professional healthcare providers and clinics that need accurate body-fat measurements for patient care.. Why behaviour changes: Clinics and health clubs already purchase and rely on Tanita scales for clinical accuracy, so a consumer version would be seen as a compatible, trusted extension of that equipment, reducing perceived risk and increasing willingness to adopt. How value is captured: Tanita would capture value through higher-margin sales to professional channels and potential licensing of the technology to medical device manufacturers, leveraging existing brand credibility.. Assumptions: Professional users are willing to recommend a consumer version to colleagues.; The consumer version can meet the same accuracy standards expected in clinical settings.; Marketing can position the product as a professional-grade tool for home use.. Predictions: Professional users would indicate intent to purchase a consumer version at a rate at least 20% higher than a generic home scale.; Sales of a consumer version would be concentrated in clinics and health clubs, with fewer than 10% of units sold to individual consumers..

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 500 participants (250 self-identified health-conscious adults and 250 professional users: clinics/health clubs). Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A (health-focused) or Condition B (professional-focused). Both conditions present a home body-fat scale with identical features (foot-to-foot BIA, 1993 model). Condition A messaging emphasizes health benefits and personal wellness; Condition B messaging emphasizes clinical accuracy and professional compatibility. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (maximum price).. Sample: 500 participants (250 health-conscious adults and 250 professional users) recruited via online panels.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition A willingness to pay ≥ Condition B willingness to pay, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition B willingness to pay ≥ Condition A willingness to pay, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Fashion vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults interested in hearing protection. Each participant sees one of two product descriptions for a hearing protection earplug: (A) Fashion/Comfort description emphasizing style, comfort, and aesthetic appeal; (B) Compliance description emphasizing safety standards, legal requirement, and suitability for specific activities (e.g., construction, outdoor recreation). After viewing the description, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) to ensure statistical power and sufficient variation in responses.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the Fashion/Comfort condition compared to the Compliance condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the Compliance condition compared to the Fashion/Comfort condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the Fashion/Comfort condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the Compliance condition, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent for the Compliance condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the Fashion/Comfort condition, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is within 1.5 points or both conditions show similar intent, the evidence is inconclusive and further testing is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because they view it as a safety necessity for outdoor activities (camping, hiking, boating) and are willing to pay a premium for peace of mind. Who benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who face remote emergency situations and want reliable rescue communication.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from relying on traditional PLBs (registered with NOAA) to a consumer product that meets FCC approval and offers real-time rescue capability, reducing fear of being unreachable.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price (e.g., $700) through retail channels, capturing margin on a single-use device rather than recurring B2B services.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. are sufficient to generate a meaningful consumer market.; FCC approval and NOAA registration requirements do not deter consumers from purchasing a consumer product.; Marketing can effectively communicate the safety benefit to individual buyers.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade PLB to outdoor enthusiasts, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a B2B version of the same technology.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'emergency rescue' as the primary reason for purchase, not cost or compatibility with existing gear..

T2: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is a convenient, low‑cost alternative to traditional PLBs, and they purchase it as a one‑time safety device rather than as a recurring service. Who benefits: Cost‑conscious consumers who want a simple, affordable way to communicate in emergencies without ongoing subscription fees.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from the hassle of NOAA registration, FCC approval, and potential service costs to a plug‑and‑play device that works immediately, reducing perceived barrier to purchase.. Test "Consumer vs B2B PLB Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Consumer Group (individual outdoor enthusiasts) and B2B Group (professional users). Each group sees a product description of a consumer-grade 406 MHz PLB priced at $700 (premium) and a B2B version priced at $400 (low-cost). They are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale and the primary reason for purchase (emergency rescue vs cost/ease).. Sample: 300 participants (150 per group) recruited via outdoor recreation forums and professional trade websites, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) and primary purchase reason (binary: emergency rescue vs cost/ease).. Predictions: T1: Consumer Group will have higher purchase intent and will cite 'emergency rescue' as the primary reason more than B2B Group.; T2: B2B Group will have higher purchase intent and will cite 'cost/ease' as the primary reason more than Consumer Group.. Decision rule: If Consumer Group purchase intent exceeds B2B Group by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale and 'emergency rescue' is the top reason for at least 60% of Consumer Group respondents, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If B2B Group purchase intent exceeds Consumer Group by at least 1.5 points and 'cost/ease' is the top reason for at least 60% of B2B Group respondents, pursue a low‑cost consumer product. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, not just speculate.; Consider existing consumer reach of Jotun’s coatings; if none, assess feasibility of entering that market.; Alternatives include expanding into consumer markets, targeting a different customer group, or maintaining current B2B focus.. T1: Individual boat owners and homeowners will adopt Jotun’s marine and protective coatings if they perceive them as a safety and durability solution for their vessels and homes, leading to repeat purchases and premium pricing. Who benefits: Jotun would benefit from higher margins and brand loyalty among individual buyers who value performance.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently lack a trusted, consumer‑friendly brand for marine protection and would switch if they see Jotun’s reputation for marine expertise and quality.. How value is captured: Jotun would capture value through direct-to-consumer sales, premium pricing, and repeat purchases of specialized coatings.. Assumptions: Individual buyers are willing to pay more for a brand they trust for marine protection.; Jotun’s existing B2B reputation transfers to consumer perception.; The market size for individual marine and homeowner coatings is sufficient to justify investment.. Predictions: A survey of individual boat owners and homeowners would show at least 30% indicating they would purchase Jotun products if priced competitively.; Direct-to-consumer sales would generate at least 15% of Jotun’s total revenue within 12 months..

T2: Homeowners and boat owners will adopt Jotun’s marine and protective coatings primarily because they are attracted to the aesthetic and design possibilities offered by decorative paints, leading to multiple coatings and premium pricing. Who benefits: Jotun would benefit from higher average order value, brand awareness among design‑focused consumers, and potential cross‑selling of decorative products.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers increasingly view paint as a design element, and Jotun’s decorative range provides a way to personalize homes and vessels, creating perceived value beyond functional protection.. How value is captured: Jotun would capture value through premium pricing for decorative products, higher margin on specialty coatings, and expanded retail presence through Jotun Multicolor Centers and online channels.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for decorative, design‑friendly coatings.; Jotun’s decorative range is differentiated enough to attract individual buyers beyond functional protection.; The market for home and boat decorative coatings is large enough to justify investment.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners and boat owners would show at least 40% indicating they would purchase Jotun decorative products if available at a premium.; Sales of decorative coatings would account for at least 20% of Jotun’s total sales within 12 months..

Test "Digital Messaging Test for Marine vs Decorative Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted digital ad campaign with two versions: Version A (marine protection messaging) and Version B (decorative design messaging). Both versions offer a limited-time discount on a Jotun product. Track click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate (purchase or sign-up).. Sample: Proposed sample: 2,000 individual homeowners and boat owners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark). Recruit via social media and email lists.. Measure: Primary measure: average CTR for each version. Secondary measure: conversion rate (purchase or sign-up) for the version with higher CTR.. Predictions: T1: Version A (marine protection) will achieve a higher CTR and conversion rate than Version B.; T2: Version B (decorative design) will achieve a higher CTR and conversion rate than Version A.. Decision rule: If Version A CTR ≥ 2.5% and Version B CTR ≤ 2.0%, proceed with a differentiated marine proposition (support T1). If Version B CTR ≥ 2.5% and Version A CTR ≤ 2.0%, proceed with a differentiated decorative proposition (support T2). If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and maintain current B2B focus.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individual marine and homeowner coatings, leveraging Jotun’s marine protection reputation. Begin with a targeted digital messaging test (Version A: marine protection) to validate demand before scaling. If the test meets the CTR threshold, proceed with direct-to-consumer sales; otherwise, maintain B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
Of the "10" series John Deere tractors introduced in 1960, the 4010 was by far the most popular, with more than 58,000 units sold from 1960 to 1963.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

T1: Consumers will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they treat lawn and garden tasks as a consumer chore, and Deere can capture value by selling a branded, differentiated unit at a premium through independent dealers, leveraging its engineering reputation to command higher prices. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small gardeners benefit from a dedicated tool for their chores; Deere benefits from premium pricing and brand extension into consumer markets.. Why behaviour changes: Growing household garden size and interest in DIY in the 1960s create demand for a dedicated lawn tractor; consumers shift from generic tools to branded, differentiated products for convenience and status.. How value is captured: Deere sells a consumer-focused tractor through dealers at higher prices than its generic tractors, and can extend its brand into new markets, potentially increasing total revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded, differentiated lawn tractor.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and sell a new consumer product.; Deere's engineering reputation allows it to command premium prices.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated consumer lawn tractor to a subset of homeowners will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than a generic tractor.; Sales of the differentiated unit will generate higher average revenue than sales of a generic unit sold through the same dealers..

T2: Consumers will purchase a differentiated consumer proposition because they view lawn and garden tasks as a status symbol and a way to demonstrate ownership, and Deere can capture value by selling a branded, differentiated unit through independent dealers, leveraging its engineering reputation to command premium prices. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small gardeners benefit from a status symbol and a way to showcase ownership; Deere benefits from brand extension and premium pricing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing middle-class affluence and the cultural importance of outdoor living in the 1960‑s create demand for lawn equipment as a status item; consumers seek to differentiate themselves through ownership of branded, differentiated tools.. How value is captured: Deere sells a consumer-focused lawn tractor at a premium price through dealers, and can extend its brand into new markets, potentially increasing total revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded, differentiated lawn tractor.; Independent dealers can effectively promote a status-oriented product.; Deere's engineering reputation allows it to command premium prices.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated consumer lawn tractor will achieve higher purchase intent among homeowners than a generic tractor.; Sales of the differentiated unit will generate higher average revenue than sales of a generic unit sold through the same dealers..

T1: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because they view it as a life-saving safety device for remote or emergency situations, and they are willing to pay a premium for reliability and compliance with NOAA/RTCM standards. Who benefits: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and individuals in remote areas who need reliable emergency communication.. Why behaviour changes: The Federal Register rule (2002) and NOAA guidelines make compliance mandatory, creating a regulatory barrier that only a certified device can clear, prompting consumers to choose a trusted brand over generic alternatives.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium-priced, certified product through retail channels, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and the FCC waiver that allowed type certification for consumer use.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of the 406 MHz PLB capability and its regulatory requirements.; They trust ACR's brand and certification status.; The price premium is acceptable for safety-critical use cases.. Predictions: In a test offering a certified 406 MHz beacon at a price 20% above a generic alternative, purchase intent among marine recreational users will be at least 15% higher than for a non-certified generic beacon.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary purchase drivers..

T2: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it offers convenience and real-time tracking, enabling them to stay connected with loved ones and receive rescue notifications, and they are willing to pay for the added safety and peace of mind. Who benefits: Travelers, outdoor workers, and families in remote areas who need continuous communication and rescue awareness.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of GPS and satellite communication makes real-time tracking desirable; consumers seek devices that provide continuous location updates and rescue notifications, creating a demand for a beacon that goes beyond a one-time emergency.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by positioning the beacon as a smart safety device with tracking and rescue capabilities, selling it through consumer electronics retailers and offering subscription services for real-time updates.. Assumptions: Consumers value continuous location tracking and rescue notifications over a single emergency signal.; The price premium for tracking features is acceptable for safety-conscious buyers.; ACR can integrate tracking software and data services into the product.. Predictions: In a test offering a tracked 406 MHz beacon at a price comparable to a standard PLB, purchase intent among outdoor workers will be at least 20% higher than for a non-tracked generic beacon.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary purchase drivers..

Test "Certified vs. Tracked 406 MHz Beacon Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a certified 406 MHz beacon described as meeting NOAA/RTCM standards and marketed for marine recreational use; Group B sees the same beacon described as offering real-time tracking and rescue notifications, marketed for outdoor workers and families. Both groups see the same product price (proposed €150). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 marine recreational users and 150 outdoor workers/families, recruited via online panels to match demographic distribution of target segments.. Measure: Purchase intent score for each group (mean of 7-point scale).. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a mean purchase intent score at least 1.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., ≥5.5 on the 7-point scale).; T2: Group B will have a mean purchase intent score at least 1.5 points higher than Group A (i.e., ≥5.5 on the 7-point scale).. Decision rule: If Group A's mean purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B's, conclude T1 is more supported. If Group B's mean purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A's, conclude T2 is more supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is framed as essential for a specific, high-risk task, users perceive it as a professional requirement rather than a lifestyle accessory, leading to greater willingness to purchase and comply.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price specialized products at premium levels and sell through B2B channels, leveraging its safety certification and brand trust to command higher margins.. Test "Fashion vs Functional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults interested in hearing protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a fashion-focused message (e.g., stylish, trendy earplugs for lifestyle use) and a premium price; Condition B receives a functional, safety-focused message (e.g., essential protection for specific high-risk activities) and a premium price. Both conditions present the same product (a designed, safety-certified earplug). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum willingness to pay.. Sample: 300 participants (150 per condition), recruited from an online panel targeting adults aged 18–45 who have purchased hearing protection in the past 12 months.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will achieve higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A’s purchase intent is at least 10 points higher than Condition B’s purchase intent, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on fashion and premium pricing. If Condition B’s purchase intent is at least 10 points higher than Condition A’s purchase intent, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on functional safety messaging and premium pricing. If the difference is less than 10 points, do not commit to a differentiated proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Who benefits: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and individuals in remote areas who need reliable emergency communication.. Why behaviour changes: The Federal Register rule (2002) and NOAA guidelines make compliance mandatory, creating a regulatory barrier that only a certified device can clear, prompting consumers to choose a trusted brand over generic alternatives.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium-priced, certified product through retail channels, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and the FCC waiver that allowed type certification for consumer use.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of GPS and satellite communication makes real-time tracking desirable; consumers seek devices that provide continuous location updates and rescue notifications, creating a demand for a beacon that goes beyond a one-time emergency.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by positioning the beacon as a smart safety device with tracking and rescue capabilities, selling it through consumer electronics retailers and offering subscription services for real-time updates.. Assumptions: Consumers value continuous location tracking and rescue notifications over a single emergency signal.; The price premium for tracking features is acceptable for safety-conscious buyers.; ACR can integrate tracking software and data services into the product.. Predictions: In a test offering a tracked 406 MHz beacon at a price comparable to a standard PLB, purchase intent among outdoor workers will be at least 20% higher than for a non-tracked generic beacon.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary purchase drivers..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Emergency vs Tracking Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing life-saving emergency capability (NOAA certification, RTCM compliance, suitable for remote or life-threatening situations). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes continuous tracking and real-time rescue notifications (GPS, location updates, rescue alerts). Both groups see a price point 20% above a generic PLB (e.g., €150). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state the primary purchase driver.. Sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced across gender and age to reflect marine recreational and outdoor user demographics. Recruitment targets individuals who have used a personal locator beacon or are interested in emergency safety gear.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase driver (open-ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (price sensitivity).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, and the majority of Group A buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary drivers.; T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Group A, and the majority of Group B buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary drivers.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than Group B, adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition (emergency capability). If Group B purchase intent ≥ 20% points higher than Group A, adopt T2‑driven consumer proposition (tracking/continuous). If the difference is ≤ 10% points, no expansion is recommended. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR already sells to individual buyers (e.g., marine recreational users) and has a B2B reputation, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for tracking or willingness to pay a premium. Run the proposed test to measure purchase intent differences between emergency and tracking messaging. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Neumann benefits by commanding premium prices and maintaining brand prestige among professionals.. Why behaviour changes: If creators perceive Neumann as the only compatible, high-quality option, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives, even if the price is higher.. How value is captured: Neumann captures value through premium pricing and brand loyalty, leveraging its professional reputation to justify higher costs.. Assumptions: Creators are price-sensitive and prioritize technical performance over aesthetics.; Compatibility with existing studio gear is a decisive purchase factor.; Professional reputation is a key differentiator in the home-studio market.. Predictions: In a survey, creators will rank compatibility and professional quality higher than price when choosing Neumann.; Willingness to pay for Neumann will be higher than for comparable non-Neumann products.; Purchase intent will be driven by the perception of Neumann as the only compatible, high-quality option..

T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers purchase Neumann products because they seek a consistent, professional experience across devices and platforms, and are willing to pay for brand reliability and ecosystem integration. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by expanding its customer base and increasing average transaction value through cross-selling of related products..
